### 19.89 Alec on the four defects, on the cost of adding a percept, and on what touches the perceptual code (2026-11-19)

His answers to §23.S.1's four defects and to the question of what a concept of order zero reads (put to him with the repair pass: the concept of `alpha` reads .65 to .75 on "beta delta").

**1. The time.** "both .where and .when are encoded in the concepts, and we will abstract over that eventually. We might want to add a time as a sinusoid encoded feeling in order to know what \"yesterday\" was numerically in LTM, that's why we added it. Maybe it can just be a part of STM that the chooser or operators have access to." So the time is kept for what it was added for, to know when a thing was; it need not be weighed by the Sigma of order zero. *As built by the repair pass:* a reading and a chunk of STM carry their `.when` as before, where the chooser and the operators can read it; the Sigma of order zero has no weight on it (rule 7). A time as a feeling coded by a sinusoid, for "yesterday" in LTM, is noted in `doc/FutureWork.md`.

**2. "an entry of four concepts? What is an entry? Can you use the glossary?"** An entry is in the glossary now. Said again in its terms: each row of LTM keeps, beside its idea, the four concepts that were most active at its moment. The concept "words" was active at every moment, since every word lights it, so it took one of the four places in every row, and the object of the sentence's own word was pushed out. The repair keeps "words" and "objects" out of a row's four concepts, and out of what a query asks of them.

**3. "When a nominated word joins words, we just add an edge to the \"words\" concept / sigma...?"** Yes, that is all that happens: one entry of the Sigma of "words". The defect was not the entry. The matrix that holds such entries was made the first time one was added, while the model was running, and making it changed the set of the model's modules, so the captured forward was traced again. It is made at construction now.

**4. "this sounds like an error you can fix. We should be predicting something en aggregate if we are doing gradient descent."** Taken: it is repaired, not left for round 5. Its cause is the next point.

**What touches the perceptual code.** "Question: the perceptual code is used exclusively to distribute codes in the hypercube, and the only thing touching that is the pi . This applies to both .what and .where (although .where is not mereological, it's just a sinusoidal band)."

*As built, that is not so.* The Sigma of order zero reads the code too: rule 7 joins the codes of the percepts present into one vector, and rule 8 has a dense Sigma of the code's width read it (both from §18.24). That is why the concept of `alpha` reads "beta delta": the letters of `beta` and `delta` cover most of `alpha`'s code, though the basic percept of `alpha` is not there at all. It is the cause of defect 4.

*Made so* (rule 62): the Sigma of order zero reads the basic percepts, each row's two values, and never the code. Then the Pi is the only thing that touches the code, for the what and for the where. This is "order zero is n:n on basic percepts" (§19.83) taken as it stands, and rule 21's "a concept starts reading only its own row, at one" taken as it stands. It makes order zero the same structure as every order above it. What is given up is §18.24's "a new percept needs no new weight": a concept no longer answers to a word it has never been given.

**The cost of adding a percept.** "is the problem constructing a mereologically correct code, or the time of making parthood links across the tensor?" Measured (the 19,821 words admitted under a profiler, 82 s):

| What an admission does | Share of the time |
| --- | ---: |
| Tests the code against every stored code, for one lying inside another (`_accidents_of_many`) | 41% |
| Finds the links, the stored forms it holds and that hold it (`_link`) | 27% |
| Settles two forms with one code (`_settle`) | 9% |
| Chooses the coordinates (`_separate_inner`) | 5% |
| Writes the changed codes (`_rewrite`) | 4% |

So it is neither the making of the code nor the writing of it. It is the two searches, each over everything stored: the test for a code inside another, and the finding of the links, which today looks through the stored forms one by one. Both can be made not to grow with the store: the links by an index of runs, and the test by one product on the device. That is item 1.5's.

### 19.90 Alec: Pi, Not, Sigma at order zero, and the Sigma monotone; one time; a slot of episodic memory; the lookup of part codes (2026-11-19)

Received while the pass that builds rule 62 was running, in answer to the report of the repair pass (§23.R).

**The order-zero signal.** "The order zero signal should be built as: Pi Not Sigma. And I made a mistake when I said it could be non-monotone, that would give it the ability to change sign, which should be restricted to not. But the important part is that Pi reads perceptual space, its two lanes get passed to Not, and those are combined into on signed lane for processing by sigma (which may process an arbitrary number of those signed values)."

*Decided* (rule 63). This withdraws rule 59, which Claude had written from his §19.83 ("after the Not layer we still have two channels, those need not be combined", and then "Conceptual weights are signed as a result, otherwise we wouldn't get negative output with no negative input"). Three steps in a fixed order:

| Step | Reads | Gives | Its weights |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pi | perceptual space (above order zero: the lanes of the concepts beneath) | for each row two values from 0 to 1, for and against | zero or above |
| Not | each row's two values | one signed value from -1 to 1 for each row, for less against; an entry of the Not gives one concept that row's pair exchanged | none of its own: an entry is there or it is not |
| Sigma | any number of those signed values | one signed value for each concept, the squashed sum | zero or above, always |

The question his earlier sentence answered, where a value below zero comes from when no input is below zero, is answered now by the Not: evidence against reaches the Sigma as a signed value below zero, and a Not entry turns evidence for into one. The Sigma itself is monotone and cannot change a sign. This returns to his §19.15 ("not carries all negation") and makes order zero the structure of rule 29 exactly.

*What it changes in what is built.* Round 4's first pass gave the order-zero Sigma for weights and against weights (§23.4, step 11): the against weights go. Round 3's Sigma had one signed weight for each input, whose part below zero was the Not entry (rule 3): a weight is now held at zero or above, and a Not entry is kept by the Not. The pass building rule 62 was sent this amendment while it ran.

*Mine, built provisionally and put to him:* what may make a Not entry. Claude's reading of "restricted to not" is that the Sigma's gradient never makes one. A Not entry is made by teaching that is the Not's own: by omission at the basic level (rule 29: "Omission teaches not"), by a Not member declared in the record of a concept's members, and above the basic level by a symbol's pair read exchanged. If he means only that the sign is kept in the Not, with the gradient free to make an entry there, the certificates of rule 63 change in one clause and the structure does not.

**1. The time.** ""carry their time" is a worrying phrase. There is one model time, we can sinusoidally encode that in one place for all readers, and let operators see it so that their logic can compare the time to that which is stamped into each concept as the .when". The phrase was Claude's, in §19.89 ("a reading and a chunk of STM carry their `.when` as before"). *Decided* (rule 64): one clock, one code of it made in one place, a stamp on each concept, and the chooser and the operators able to compare the present time with a stamp. What the source has now, how many clocks and how many places that encode a time, is being counted (§23.T); the change is round 6's.

**2. The slots.** "Entry should be slot in episodic memory ( the idea is semantic memory). Most active is clearly not useful; perhaps least expected, or sentence dominant such as np, vp, ?" *Decided as far as it goes* (rule 65). The term is *slot*: a row of LTM keeps an idea, which is semantic memory, and a few slots, which are episodic memory. "Entry" is then left to mean one thing, an entry of a matrix (a for entry, a Not entry). The slots are no longer the most active concepts. *Open, his question mark; Claude's first choice is the least expected:* the concepts whose value is furthest from what the expectation gave. It needs no parse, so it holds for a mind with the basic level alone; the words every sentence has are expected and leave the slots to the words that set this moment apart; and the sentence's constituents are already what the idea is made of. Both are measured in round 6c on the question of rule 60, whether a question on top of the STM stack finds the row that answers it, before either is built. *To rename with it:* the source's column `slots` of a row of LTM holds the ideas, and `episodic_concepts` the slots.

**3 and 4.** "good pre allocation" (the matrix of a concept's members made at construction, §19.89, 3); "ok" (the repair of the fourth defect, which rule 62 is).

**The lookup of part codes.** "Let me think about how to speed up the part code lookup. Since they are all matrices, why can't we just run the comparison algorithm itself on the part powerset of the code being inserted, and take the intersection of those results?"

It can, and measured it is the faster way. A stored code holds the new code exactly when it holds the code of each of the new form's parts, so the intersection of the results for the parts is one test of the whole code against the stored codes; taken the other way, it gives the stored codes that lie inside the new one. Each candidate found is then checked for the run: with the run it is a link, without it an accident. Measured on the 19,821 words, at 64 and 64, on the processor (`lookup_split.py` in the scratch directory; no source changed):

| | Seconds over the 19,821 admissions |
| --- | ---: |
| The links as built: every stored form looked through for the run (`WordIdentity._link`) | 20.3 |
| One test of the new code against the stored codes, both ways | 3.0 |
| The check of the candidates it gives for the run | 0.04 |
| The test for accidents as built (`_accidents_of_many`): the comparison 10.8, reading out the pairs 2.3, sorting links from accidents 0.6 | 13.7 |

- The one test finds every link: of 7,863 holders and 51,808 parts, none is missed. It gives 137,803 candidates, of which 78,132 have no run; those are the accidents that the repair then removes, so the same test serves both searches at a form's introduction.
- The test for accidents is not costly for the new form. It is costly because a repair changes codes and each changed form is tested again against the whole store: 29,293 tests of 452,169 forms, 23 forms for each admission. *Not measured:* kept by part, as he puts it, one list of forms for each coordinate, the test of a form given one coordinate need only look at the forms that have that coordinate, and an intersection can begin from its rarest part, so neither search grows with the store.
- It is an equal-results change and is item 1.5's, where the numbers are recorded.

His answers to the three questions of §19.90 and to §23.T's census of time.

**On the two orders of the Pi and the Sigma** (the same hour, before these): "Sorry for having you code something I did not wish to finalize; running pi and sigma in parallel would not build concepts of percepts/symbols, which is the basic model of human cognition." *Claude's reading:* as built until rule 62 the Pi and the Sigma of order zero each read the perceptual code, side by side, so a concept was a sum over the code's coordinates and not a concept of any percept. The series Pi, Not, Sigma is the model: the Pi makes percepts and symbols, and the Sigma makes concepts of them. Rule 57's trial, a Sigma driving the wholes half of a code from above, is the one place left where a Sigma would stand beside the Pi; it is a trial in tests and stays one unless he withdraws it.

**The time.** Quoting §23.T's "No operator is given the present": "We need one integer clock and one sinusoidal encoding of it. They should be given the present, as sinusoidally encoded. They will see concepts that may have used that value, so they will need a comparator to know how far back in history the concept they have recalled is." *Decided* (rule 64, restated; certificate 55). One whole-number clock, so the second clock of LTM and STM0 goes. One encoder, so the encoders made on the spot go. The chooser and the operators are given the present in the code, and a comparator that takes the present and a stamp and gives how far back the stamp is. A stamp is no longer rewritten as an age before they see it. *Mine:* the comparator gives the distance in ticks, exactly within the code's range. Round 6 builds it.

**Q3, the stamp of a concept.** ""its rows stamp". If you mean the .where or .when of the percepts that get muxed to form the concept, we should treat the concept as opaque always, so of course keep its parts together." *Decided* (rule 64): a concept keeps its `.where` and its `.when`. What the source does now, setting the time of a row to zero when it is promoted to a concept (`MemoryConsolidation`), goes.

**Q1, what makes a Not entry.** "the gradient should be able to make a not entry, that is the implicit definition." *Decided* (rule 63, restated; certificate 51 (d)). Claude's reading in §19.90, that the gradient never makes one, is withdrawn. Implicitly, the gradient makes a Not entry where teaching takes a for entry down to zero and further; explicitly, omission makes one at the basic level. The Sigma's weight is still never below zero: the size of an entry is the Sigma's and its sign is the Not's. This is the pair of §19.88 again, implicit before explicit, as for symbols and for concepts. The pass building rule 62 was sent it while it ran.

**The lookup, thinned.** "Part code lookup can be made even more sparse by thinning the powerset under the assumption that the existing corpus is correct (so try removing the strict parts of the powerset)."

Tried, and it holds. With the stored forms kept by part, one list of forms for each part, a form's holders are the meeting of the lists of its parts; and since a stored form that holds a part holds every part of that part, only the form's maximal parts need be met, those that are a strict part of no other part of it. Measured on the full store of 19,821 words for 3,000 forms drawn from it (`lookup_thin.py` in the scratch directory; no source changed):

| Way of finding a form's holders | Parts met | Milliseconds a form | Holders missed | Candidates that are no holder |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Every stored form looked through for the run, as built | | 2.25 | 0 | 0 |
| One test of the whole code against the stored codes (§19.90) | | 0.23 | 0 | 0 |
| Lists by part, every part of the form | 13.6 | about 0.005 | 0 | 0 |
| Lists by part, the maximal parts only | 3.3 | about 0.002 | 0 | 0 |

- All four give exactly the same 17,163 holders. In a store with no accident the whole-code test gives no candidate that is not a holder, which is rule 61 seen from this side.
- The lists are about 450 times faster than the look through the store and about 45 times faster than the whole-code test, and they do not grow with the store: the shortest list of a form has 83 forms on average.
- Thinning takes the parts met from 13.6 to 3.3. In this scratch form, finding which parts are maximal costs about as much as it saves (0.006 ms against 0.003); kept as rows of a matrix on the device it is a product a quarter the size. The last two rows are at the edge of what the clock resolves.
- *Not measured:* the same lists kept by coordinate for the test of accidents after a repair, which is where the remaining cost of an admission is (§19.90).

It is item 1.5's, recorded there.

### 19.92 Alec: the clock's code is exposed on the model beside it (2026-11-19)

"One integer clock, but the arch can read the sinusoid encoding of it as exposed adjacently ( on the model )."

*Decided* (rule 64, certificate 55 (f)). The clock is one integer on the model. Its sinusoidal code is made once, when the clock advances, and is held on the model next to the integer. The architecture reads the present there: the chooser, the operators, and whatever stamps a `.when`. No reader encodes the clock for itself. In the source today the nearest thing is the shared `model.when_encoding` with its mirror of the clock (§23.T); round 6's step 16 makes it the one place.

### 19.93 Alec: intersection and union at the basic level, conjunction and disjunction at the symbolic; top-down conceptual attention drives the analysis (2026-11-19)

His answers to the two points left open with him.

**On graded values, the grammar's least and greatest against the Pi's product** (open point 8 of §21). "I like the intersection/union operations as subsymbolic (basic level) and conjunction/disjunction at the symbolic level. I don't think that leaves room for an and/or, but in general we can expose different operations to the languages and see what UG picks." *Decided.* The two are two things at two levels and are not made to agree. Intersection and union, the least and the greatest of graded values, are operations of the basic level, below symbols. Conjunction and disjunction are the symbolic level's: the Pi, a row that needs all of its members, and the Sigma, a concept that any member may be enough for. No third pair named `and` and `or` stands beside them. More than one operation may be offered to a grammar, and which it uses is learned.

**On rule 57, the Sigma driving the wholes half of a code.** "We want top-down conceptual attention, I think that can drive the what/where pathways over both particles and properties. The sigma driving wholes (properties) was an early version of that, but we need something driving that analysis top-down just like synthesis drives bottom-up part construction. Please make sure that we have the wired version thereof, as with the part construction." *Decided.* Rule 57's Sigma is withdrawn as the early version. What drives the analysis from above is conceptual attention: the request over concepts, carried down onto the what and the where, over both towers, the parts and the properties. It is the counterpart of the synthesis, which builds rows upward from parts.

*Claude's reading of "the wired version", to be confirmed:* computed by the structure's own matrices and no others. The way up is the first Pi's entries over a row's parts and its properties, then the Not, then the Sigma. The way down is those same entries read by their transposes: a requested concept gives its share to its rows through the Sigma's weights and the Not, and each row gives its share to every member, the parts on the part tower and the properties on the property tower, and to its where. No second set of weights is learned for the way down, and nothing is looked up on the host. Rule 36 has this for a row's activity and its where; it is now said for both towers (rule 36, certificate 56; round 6, step 3). Round 5's trial of rule 57 goes.

### 19.94 Alec: the Not is a layer of options; nothing is one to one; the Pi analyses wholes; on the sparse Sigma and on expectation (2026-11-19)

His answers to the review of round 4's second pass (§23.4.1), numbered as its four findings.

**1. The regression.** "we will figure it out". It is traced first in round 4's third pass.

**2. Adding entries to the sparse Sigma.** "I don't know what to do about adding entries to the sparse Sigma. It should be sparse at higher orders for sure, but i'm not sure about at the basic level." *Open, his.* Two things are apart here. That an addition grows slower as more is stored is a defect of how the entries are indexed, and round 4's third pass repairs it whatever is decided. Whether the Sigma of order zero is sparse is a question of what can be learned:

| | Dense at order zero | Sparse at order zero |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What the gradient can do | connect any row to any concept | move only the entries that are written |
| Numbers stored, lesson (4,096 rows) | 16.8 million, about 200 MB with the optimizer | two for each row and concept, 0.59 MB |
| Numbers stored, default capacity (262,144 rows) | 69 billion, which no machine here holds | about 30 MB |
| What it needs beside the gradient | nothing | something that offers an entry before the gradient can use it |

So at the default capacity it is stored sparse, and the open question is what offers an entry. Today: a concept's own row at one, a declared member, and a member recorded at weight zero, which is written at zero for the gradient to size and to choose its option. *Claude's first choice, not built:* when a concept is taught in a reading, the rows present in that reading are offered to it as entries at zero; that is dense over what occurs together and sparse over everything else. To be tried in round 5 with the order of learning, by observation first.

**3. `teach_omission`.** "removing teach_omission is fine, but do tell me what it does: if its about "not" creation, then we have the two paths." It is about the making of a Not entry and nothing else. Given a set of readings, it finds those where a concept was read above a half and did not come; each row present there, and present in no reading where the concept did come, has the concept's entry on it made a Not entry. It was a rule beside the gradient for conditioned inhibition (A gives the concept, A with X does not, so X becomes a Not entry). Nothing in the model called it, and the gradient makes the same entries by itself in certificate 23's cases (§23.4.1). *Decided:* removed; the two paths are the gradient and a declared Not member (rule 63).

**4. The Not, and one to one.** "the not is a weight that swaps the two channels. It should actually be a layer that provides options, so that concepts can choose value or not-value (since we want to allow concepts of absence as well as concepts of presence). please do not enforce that one percept or symbol goes to one concept, or that the subsequent PI must collect one sigma (as before). We have identity/generalization on a hypercone, and set creation / bifrcation on a hyperplane."

*Decided* (rules 63, 21 and 10; certificate 51 (e) and (f)).

- The Not is a layer. For each row it offers the value and the not-value, and a concept's entry chooses one. This is what the second pass built in effect (an entry's sign), now named as what it is; a concept of absence reads the not-value.
- Nothing is one to one. "Each row brings one concept" and "a symbol brings one concept" are how a row and a symbol start. A row or a symbol may be read by any number of concepts, a concept may read any number of rows or symbols, and a row of the Pi above may read any number of concepts. The third pass was told to list every place in the source that assumes one.
- *The two geometries* (his; recorded in the glossary). The Pi is identity and generalization on a hypercone: a row is a region about a direction of the space beneath, and what falls inside it is the same thing. The Sigma is the making of sets and bifurcation on a hyperplane: a weighted sum divides the space beneath in two, and what lies on one side is the set.

**The Pi and wholes.** "The analysis from above is conceptual attention over both towers. We should make sure that PI is capable of analysis for wholes just as aggregation can do synthesis for parts." *Taken* (certificate 56 (e)). As built since round 3c (rule 52), a part's code is built by joining, the greatest, and a whole's by narrowing: a whole defined by other wholes is their least, a basic percept's row is a product over its run of parts and each of its wholes read where the run lies, and a form's wholes half is at or below each of its wholes'. So the Pi's product is the analysis: each property divides, and the row is what is left inside all of them. What is not yet shown is the way down over wholes, the request reaching each property of a row through the Pi's own entries; round 6 shows it.

**On expectation.** "The expectation test: please summarize the current state of expectation, I am forgetting a bit with so many recent iterations. If 1.8's expectation map from basic percepts through not to concepts and then back down through reconstruction was expectation, then a free Pi whose every row starts with a small weight on every order-zero concept would learn to expect missing information evenatually." (Then: "("through Not to concepts", I will try to capitalize operations in the future)".)

*The state of it, from the source and `doc/ExpectationRetention.md`:*

1. *It is a map beside the main path, and not the path itself.* The main path is percepts, the first Pi, the Not, the Sigma, concepts; the way back is the reconstruction. `expect` is a separate learned map that reads the observed concepts of order zero of a sentence, on both lanes, and gives expected values for the same concepts: a field to a field (`expect_stack`, a free Pi of 64 rows and then a Sigma that starts at zero).
2. *Its teacher is omission.* Where training hides some of a sentence's words, `expect` is given the concepts of what is left and is compared with the concepts of the whole sentence. A sentence with nothing hidden teaches it nothing.
3. *Who reads it.* Its field is published once when a sentence opens, and attention, the chooser and retrieval read it. `intuit` is the same field carried up the orders. Before each look it forecasts what should be at the look's place from everything seen elsewhere; what the look returns beyond that is the excess and what was forecast beyond it is the omission, which `attend` reads.
4. *It supplies no missing percept yet.* It expects concepts. Nothing carries an expected concept down to percepts, so where input is withheld the reconstruction is not filled (certificate 24's blind spot: none of five bytes filled). Rule 30 and round 5 build that: a spread on the structure's own rows, up from the part that is present and down to the part that is missing.
5. *Two more reads exist beside it:* the read of a field to one point, the idea, taught by the idea that comprehension concludes (`idea_stack`); and a predictor over symbols with the times of recent sentences (`SymbolExpectation`).

*On whether the free Pi would learn in the end.* Probed by Claude at the map's start (`expect_probe.py` in the scratch directory), 44 concepts, two present at .76:

| | Concepts exact (the others at nothing) | Every other concept at .70, as before rule 62 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| A row of the Pi, mean | .0016 | .42 |
| Greatest gradient at the Pi | .067 | .64 |
| Greatest gradient at the Sigma | .012 | 2.3 |

So he is right that a gradient reaches it: it is not nothing at the start, about a tenth at the Pi and a two-hundredth at the Sigma. What the second pass measured after 200 presentations is that it had not learned, and that the Pi's weights had grown from .011 to .05 on every concept, where a row is at nothing. *Claude's reading, not measured:* a row is lowered far more cheaply by a weight on a concept that is absent (whose membership is at the floor) than by one that is present, so the first thing the error teaches is weight on the absent concepts, and that closes the rows. A product over every concept says "all of these are here", and with exact concepts they never are. Whether it recovers with more presentations is not known.

*Three ways, put to Alec:* round 5's spread on nominated rows carries the case of a word expected from the word beside it, and the map is measured again after it (Claude's first choice); the map's rows are started on a few concepts each; or the map is left as it is and given many more presentations, to see.

### 19.95 Alec: the Sigma as the fallback over properties; how a sparse Sigma grows implicitly; expectation taught by the reconstruction, in stages (2026-11-19)

**The way down over wholes.** Quoting §19.94's "What is not yet shown is the way down over wholes, the request reaching each property through the Pi's own entries": "If that doesn't work, we need to revert to the sigma to do discrimination over the set of properties." *Decided.* Round 6 shows the way down over properties by the Pi's own entries (certificate 56 (a), (b) and (e)), and says plainly whether it holds. If it does not, rule 57's Sigma over the set of properties is built in its place. It stays withdrawn until then.

**How a sparse Sigma grows without MTM.** "we have MTM doing promotion for explicit, but implicit has no expose to grow with a sparse interconnection. is there some way to test exposure randomly over the missing entries to see if any develops a strong weight, and prune if not? I think we had a full PI from which we pruned the least significant weights, and we could do a similar thing for Sigma, but Im not sure that is robust (perhaps small weights have a large effect). Thoughts? A full matrix with regularization would be best if there were not millions of percepts and concepts at the basic level."

*Claude's thoughts, as asked; nothing of it is built, and it is tried in tests first (rule 67).*

1. *Random exposure is not needed, because the gradient of a missing entry can be known exactly.* The entry of concept c on row r receives, in one reading, the error that reaches c times the signed value of r. That is nothing unless r is present in the reading and an error reaches c. A sentence has a few rows present, so over all the missing entries the gradient of a reading is nothing but on (the rows present) by (the concepts an error reaches): tens of numbers, not billions. An entry drawn at random on an absent row would learn nothing in that reading either. So the exposure can be exact where it can matter at all.
2. *That makes the sparse matrix the full matrix with regularization, stored without its zeros.* Under a penalty on the size of each weight, a weight of the full matrix that stands at zero leaves zero only when the gradient that gathers on it is greater than the penalty; and a weight returns to zero when its gradient no longer holds it against the penalty. So: keep, for the pairs of a present row and a taught concept, the gradient the missing entry would have had, gathered over readings; write the entry when what has gathered exceeds the penalty; remove an entry when the penalty brings it to zero. One number, the penalty, governs growing and pruning, and it is the penalty of rules 15 and 22.
3. *His doubt about pruning by the least weight is right, and this is what answers it.* A small weight with a large effect has a large gradient holding it, and the penalty does not bring it to zero. Pruning by the size of a weight removes it; pruning by the penalty does not. Where a measure of an entry's worth is wanted for a report, it is the weight times its gradient, or the entry's mean contribution over the readings where its concept is used, and not the weight alone.
4. *What bounds it.* The gathered gradients are kept only for pairs that have occurred together, in a table of fixed size that drops the weakest; a concept's own row and its declared members are never pruned (as the structure of a meta concept is never thinned).
5. *Where the full matrix can be afforded it is the measure:* at the lesson's size the full matrix under the same penalty is 200 MB, so the trial is the sparse form against the full one, the same entries and the same readings.

**Expectation.** "Regarding expectation, can we let it be taught by the reconstruction? so it is a form of intermediate prediction, or a reconstruction that happens in stages: we are predicting the state of percepts, concepts, and output. using the existing architecture will allow us to to sparse in interconnection, which should help amplify the salience."

*Taken as the direction* (rule 66; round 5, step 1). Expectation is no map of its own. It is the reconstruction, made in stages on the structure's own matrices: what is expected of the percepts, of the concepts at each order, and of the output, each compared with what the whole sentence has at that stage. Its teacher is the reconstruction's error. Where training hides some of a sentence, the error at what was hidden is what teaches it. The free map of item 1.8 (`expect_stack`) goes, and with it the question of §19.94 about its free Pi. Its interconnection is the structure's, which is sparse, and that is his reason: "which should help amplify the salience".

*One thing Claude holds to in building it, put to him:* what is expected stays apart from what is observed. The same matrices are run a second time, the spread of rules 23 to 27 and 30, and what it gives is written as expected and never as evidence. Without that, the error at a hidden word would teach the concept of that word to read the row of the word beside it, and the concept would then be present for a word that is not there, which is what rule 62 removed (`alpha` reading on "beta delta"). So the error at what was hidden teaches the row that holds the two together, the symbol above, which MTM nominates when they recur and which the gradient may also grow (rule 67), and not an entry from one word's row to the other word's concept.

*What it replaces, to be said by round 5:* the cost `expectation.concepts` becomes the second stage of the reconstruction; attention's forecast of a look, the chooser, retrieval and `intuit` read the spread's field where they read `expect`'s; the read of a field to an idea (`idea_stack`) is another thing and stays; `test_81` is the certificate of the second stage.

### 19.96 Alec: expectation is not evidence; how it joins the signal; whether intuit has a map of its own (2026-11-19)

"please verify that intuit still has a map of its own. expectation is not counted as evidence, it is just removing some of the burden from later layers. it should be used only to guess at network activation. I think we had some good justification for how to integrate it with the overall signal previously; it stops a gradient, but passes the entire signal".

**Expectation is not evidence.** *Decided* (rule 66; it was Claude's condition in §19.95, and is now his). What is expected is a guess at the network's activation and is never counted as evidence.

**How it joins the signal: found, and kept.** It is the form decided on 2026-10-19 and 20 (`doc/ExpectationRetention.md`, "Expectation across the architecture"), and rule 66 changes where the expected values come from and nothing of this:

- *A gain on what arrives, never a subtraction from it.* The content a reader receives is the arriving signal times attention's gain times expectation's gain. No image of the prediction is added to the content or taken from it.
- *The whole signal passes.* The gain is one number for each symbol and not one for each coordinate, so it changes how strong a thing is and not what it is: "a cat whose every feature but its whiskers was predicted would become a whiskers vector" otherwise. At full confidence and no surprise the gain falls to a floor, and the thing is still seen.
- *The gradient is stopped at the gain.* The whole of the gain is detached, "so the predictor receives gradient only through the residual, never through the gain; otherwise it could mispredict to brighten the signal or over-predict to silence it".
- *Beside the gain, the expected activation primes selection:* attention, the chooser and retrieval read it detached. "It is never added to comprehension, so top-down expectation reaches perception only through attention ... a hallucination here is a concept conceived without perceptual evidence, not a percept predicted into existence."
- *What is read beside the content* is the residual on two lanes, the excess and the omission, which salience, retention and attention read.
- As shipped the two gains are zero (`perceptExpectationGain`, `symbolExpectationGain`) and the prime is on.

**Whether `intuit` has a map of its own: it has not** (read in the source at `ab1588abea`).

- The operator `intuit` of thought (`ThoughtFaces.intuit`, `IntuitionField.read`) has no parameter. It takes the field that `expect` published when the sentence opened (`_expected_knowing`, order zero), detached, joins it by the greatest into its stream's knowing at the observed places, and carries it up the orders by the closure of the definitions (`FieldProjection.close`). This is his decision of 2026-11-17, "expect and intuit are one map" (1.8 §68.53). So when item 1.8's free map goes, `intuit` has nothing of its own left to read: under rule 66 it reads the spread's field, which is already carried over the orders.
- A module named for intuition does hold weights, and it is another thing: `IntuitionLayer` (`ConceptualSpace.intuition`, room for 4,096), two sparse banks, one weight for each literal of a remembered rule's antecedent and one for each rule, started at one and held at zero or above. They are read where thought applies a stored rule (`Intuition.execute` and `evaluate`, behind `implication` and the selection of a rule), not by `intuit`. Rule 66 does not touch it.
- *One thing found that is put to him.* `intuit` writes what is expected into knowing: the expected field is joined by the greatest into the stream's evidence, and the result is marked as written knowing of the kind "intuition". That is the one place where what is expected becomes something later operators read as evidence. It is an act thought chooses, it is detached, and it is labelled. *Claude's first choice:* it stays, as the one deliberate taking of a guess, since what it does is exactly "guess at network activation" for the operators that follow; the alternative is that `intuit` writes to the expected field alone and never to knowing.

### 19.97 Alec: intuit has the Pi, Not, Sigma that stands outside the architecture; what it gives is not "the expected field" (2026-11-19)

Told that `intuit` has no map of its own (§19.96): "so if expectation comes from the arch, please let intuit have the pi-not-sigma that exists outside of the architecture. We should not call it "the expected field", since it is called from an operator, whereas expect is built in to a model parameter."

*Decided* (rule 68; rule 66 amended). There are two things again, and they differ by where they stand and by who calls them:

| | Expectation (`expect`) | Intuition (`intuit`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where it is computed | in the architecture: the spread on the structure's own Pi, Not and Sigma (rule 66) | outside the architecture: a Pi, Not, Sigma of its own, from concepts to concepts |
| What turns it on | built in; a parameter of the model | an operator, when thought calls it |
| What it gives | the expected field, a guess at activation; never evidence | the intuited field, which the operator writes into knowing, marked as intuition |
| Taught by | the reconstruction, in stages | *open, below* |

So the free map of item 1.8 (`expect_stack`, a free Pi of 64 rows and a Sigma) does not go, as §19.95 had it: it becomes `intuit`'s own, and is no longer read as expectation. This undoes the fold of 2026-11-17 ("expect and intuit are one map", 1.8 §68.53) and returns to his two networks of System 1 of 2026-11-12, with expectation now the architecture's. The question of §19.96, whether `intuit` may write into knowing, is closed by it: what `intuit` writes is intuition's and not expectation's, so "expectation is never evidence" has no exception.

*Open, put to him: what teaches `intuit`'s map.* Today its only teacher is omission, the concepts of the whole sentence where words were hidden, which is expectation's lesson. *Claude's first choice* is his of 2026-11-12, approved then and removed with the fold: `intuit` "learns from conceptualizing or thinking about the input", so its teacher is the field that thought leaves (with the cost of the output), and omission teaches expectation alone. Until he answers, round 5 keeps the map with the teacher it has.

*Carried with it:* the start of its free Pi. Each row starts with a small weight on every concept, and with exact concepts such a row is at nothing and learns slowly if at all (§19.94). Round 5 measures it and starts each row on a few concepts if that is what it takes (*mine*).

### 19.98 Alec: what makes what; and no rule on a walk that is there to pass a measure (2026-11-20)

On the report of round 4's fifth pass (§23.4.4), two worries.

**"symbols are not yet split from concepts."** "That worries me. I hope you know that symbols (and percepts) are created from concepts via Pi , and concepts are created from symbols and percepts via Not and Sigma."

*That is the design, and it is what §21 says* (rules 2, 3, 10, 29, 62, 63). A Pi makes what needs all of its members: at order zero the basic percepts, over the parts and the properties of perceptual space, and above it the symbols, over the concepts beneath. The Not and a Sigma make the concepts: at order zero from the basic percepts, above it from the symbols. The sentence he quotes was about how far the source has come, and should have said so:

| | The design | The source at `ff022b3bfe` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Order zero | Pi over perceptual space gives basic percepts; Not; sparse Sigma gives concepts | built so (§23.4.1 to §23.4.4) |
| Above order zero | Pi over concepts gives symbols; Not; sparse Sigma gives concepts | not yet: the store that computes the higher concepts still reads each concept's own two lanes as if they were that concept's symbol, one for one, and joins them by the least and the greatest. The symbols' own table and Pi exist since the fifth pass and nothing reads them yet. The sixth pass makes the store read them, then replaces the least and the greatest by the Not and the Sigma |

*One word of his sentence Claude reads with care, and puts to him:* "percepts ... created from concepts via Pi". As built and as rule 2 has it, a basic percept is a row of the first Pi over perceptual space, its parts and its properties, and no concept is among its members; it is the symbols that are rows over concepts. If he means that a percept above the basic level is a row over concepts, that is what the source calls a symbol. If he means that basic percepts too are to be made from concepts, that is not built and not in the rules.

**A rule that a walk may not return to a state it has been in.** "And 8m worried about rules like "A walk may not take an unfocus that returns its table to a state it has already been in.", as that seems very unbiological, presumably tweaking the animal behavior just to get it to pass tests. What problem is it designed to solve?"

*The problem.* It is the one he named on 2026-11-18 (`doc/FutureWork.md`, "A record of the places attention has examined"): "Nothing then records that its place was examined, so the same look is legal again, and a fresh model repeats it until the sentence's acts are spent." Measured in §23.L: a walk descends onto a word, then takes the unfocus, which puts the table back exactly as it was; nothing has changed, so the same descend wins again, and the two repeat to the cap of 32 steps. Which of the two wins the first time is a difference of a thousandth between two scores of an untaught chooser. In a run where it falls the wrong way the model reads no word of the later sentences, and that was a run in two or three. So it is not a test that it fails: the lesson is the measure of whether the model reads at all, and with the loop the measure said nothing (0 to 53 words on one source).

*He is right about the rule.* The fourth pass's rule (no unfocus at the step right after the focus it undoes) and the wider one sent to the sixth pass are prohibitions written into the table of legal acts. They remove the loop and do not give the walk what it lacks, which is his own words: "some record of having examined a particular place". The mechanism that the science of attention has for it is graded and is not a prohibition: inhibition of return, a place just attended is less salient for a while, so that looking moves on (Posner and Cohen, 1984; Klein, 2000; cited from memory, to be checked before they enter the docs).

*Done at once.* The wider rule is withdrawn from the sixth pass before it was built. *Kept, marked as a scaffold, and put to him:* the fourth pass's narrower rule. With it the lesson reads 63.6 words of 64 over 12 runs; without it there is no measure to compare the remaining rounds on. It goes when round 6 builds the record (rule 69), and sooner if he says so.

*For round 6* (rule 69, *mine, from his words of 2026-11-18; put to him*): the record of what a walk has examined is a lowering of that place's salience that fades over the walk's steps, read by the chooser as one more reason and never as a mask. It answers the question the future-work note left open, "whether it forbids a second look, or lowers its score", by lowering.

### 19.99 Alec: no unfocus rule at all; the chooser's own log in STM; teaching by successive approximation; behaviour chains, and a song over the output (2026-11-20)

His answers to §19.98.

**Percepts.** "Your check on percepts: correct, they come from the two mereological towers of percepts." *Settled:* a basic percept is a row of the first Pi over the part tower and the property tower; symbols are the rows over concepts.

**The unfocus rule.** "The unfocus rule is probably unnecessary, and a focused state may be good context to move focus to the right until sentence end. The narrow rule should also be removed." *Decided.* Both go: the wider rule was never built, and the fourth pass's narrower one (§23.4.3, part E) is removed by the sixth pass, with nothing put in its place. The loop of §23.L is then back, and the lesson's wide spread with it; that is accepted, and what answers it is the next three paragraphs and not a mask. *His thought on the walk itself:* once focused on a word, that state is the context from which to move the focus to the right, word by word, to the sentence's end; the way out of a focus is on, not back.

**Teaching it.** "Animals are taught via successive approximation under behavioral conditioning paradigms, I imagine the same might work here; we can't teach focus directly, but we can reward behaviors that require a successively narrow focus." *Taken as the way attention is taught* (rule 70). No rule says where to look. The lessons are ordered so that each can only be done with a narrower focus than the one before, and what is rewarded is the behaviour, by its outcome.

**What the chooser needs to learn from.** "I'm guessing that some log of the animals behavior (from the chooser) or what it experiences in the environment might be useful as episodic state, in STM at least, that the chooser has in its domain so that the gradient can teach actions based on that. I would expect long-term behaviors to be learned as behavior chains that can be replayed in STM or LTM , and eventually in concepts." *Taken* (rule 69, rewritten). The record of where a walk has looked is not a lowering of salience built in by hand, as Claude wrote it in §19.98; it is a log of what the walk has done and what came of it, held in STM, in the chooser's domain, and what the chooser does with it is learned. A behaviour that lasts is a chain of acts, replayed from STM or from LTM, and in the end held as concepts.

**A test of sequence.** "Let's add a test for sequence learning in the sense of "singing a song over the output". For 1.6, counting would be a good test of that that might be simpler than moving focus reliably over words." *Taken* (certificate 59; item 1.6's plan and the todo). A learned sequence is produced over the output, each item from the one before with no input between; in item 1.6 the song is counting.

*Mine, put to him, each built on the first choice until he says otherwise:*

1. *What the log holds:* for each of the walk's last steps, the act taken, the place it was taken at, and what it returned (the words found, the excess and the omission of the look). In STM as chunks of the walk, not in a store of its own.
2. *Whether a move of the focus to the right is an act of its own.* Today a walk leaves a word by the unfocus and descends again; there is no act that carries the focus from one word to the next. *First choice:* round 6's looks give it (a look is a place, rule 32, and the next look's place is asked by the chooser), so no new act is added to the old table.
3. *What the lesson measures meanwhile.* With no rule against the loop the lesson's words found run from nothing to most of them by the draw of the initialization. It is still reported over 12 runs, with the walks that repeat a state; rounds are judged by their own certificates until round 6.

### 19.100 Alec: the log is conceptual activation in episodic memory; attend() alone; what guides the choosers today (2026-11-20)

His answers to the three readings of §19.99.

**1. The log.** "If the log is holding act, place, etc, then make the log conceptual activation stored in episodic memory, so that you are not just bolting on memory and structures to the algorithm. Feel free to create those concepts or use the grammar ones already there, and increase episodic memory from 4. You may also have to allow it in the operator domain; p,ease confirm the operators have a nonlinear network guiding choice that has such a domain currently."

*Decided* (rule 69). The log is no structure of its own. What a walk did at a step is the activation of concepts, kept in the slots of episodic memory (rule 65) of that step's chunk: the concept of the act, the concepts of its place, and the concepts of what it returned. The grammar's concepts for its operators and arguments are used where they exist, and concepts are declared for what has none. A row has room for more than four slots.

*What guides the choosers today, checked in the source at `2beec0847a`:*

| Chooser | The network | What it reads for each candidate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compose and `attend` (one object, `OperationSelectionLayer.chooser`) | With the key `transformChooser` set to `mlp`, as it is in the lesson's configuration and in the main ones (`BasicModel.xml`, the corpus and ladder configurations): a contextual network, one hidden layer with a nonlinearity and then a score (`MLPTransformChooser`). Where the key is absent the source's default is a linear score, the inner product with an anchor for each act, and that has no nonlinearity. | The state of the slot, a vector of the code's width (for `attend` the key of the bracket, "the prefix understood at this look", with the attention context added to it); the candidate's output, the same width; a learned vector of 8 for the act; a code of 8 for the position. For thought, 29 numbers more. |
| Thought | *Corrected (§23.T.1):* not a network of its own. The class `SelectedThoughtChooser` is built nowhere; thought's choice is scored by the same chooser as compose and `attend`. | The roles of the root, the active chunk and the candidate; bounded numbers on what is held; the level and the pressure. |
| Generate (`GeneratePolicy`) | Linear over the top chunk, with a small network over five numbers of the menu. | The top chunk and the menu's numbers. |

So there is a nonlinear network guiding the choice for compose, `attend` and thought in the configurations in use. *It does not have such a domain yet:* none of the three reads the slots of episodic memory. They read state vectors, and thought reads four summary numbers of a row of LTM, never the concepts a row's slots hold. The way in exists for `attend`: it takes a context that is added to its keys (`AttentionContext.project`, linear, starting at zero), and that is where the slots of the walk's last chunks enter.

*Mine, put to him:* the slots of a chunk are raised from 4 to 8 by the key `episodicConcepts`, to be measured; which concepts of a moment fill the slots that the log does not take stays the question of rule 65.

**2. The acts.** "you can just use attend() , I don't see a need for explicit focus and unfocus operators". *Decided* (rule 69; round 6). A walk has one act of attention, `attend`, which asks for what it wants to look at (rule 35). The table's focus (descend) and unfocus go with the table in round 6, and nothing takes their place: moving on to the next word is a request, and so is returning to the whole sentence.

**3. The grades.** "good." *Decided* (rule 70): the sentence, then its words in order, then a word's parts.

### 19.101 Alec: there is no "symbol of a concept" (2026-11-20)

Asked by Claude (§23.4.5, finding 2): "Should a word's order-zero concept get its symbol when its row is nominated?" His answer:

"* a basic percept or symbol is created implicitly by PI or when nominated by MTM when recognizing that their constituents always occur together.
* a concept is created implicitly by Sigma or when nominated by MTM when recognizing that the objects form a kind.

So the rubric of "the symbol of a concept" suggests a 1:1 correspondance that is no longer valid."

*Decided* (rule 71; rules 10 and 20 amended). The question was wrongly put, and so was what three passes built towards. A row of a Pi, a basic percept or a symbol, exists because its constituents always occur together: the Pi makes it implicitly, or MTM nominates it on recognizing that. A concept exists because its objects form a kind: the Sigma makes it implicitly, or MTM nominates it on recognizing that. Nothing makes a symbol *for* a concept, and nothing makes a concept *for* a row beyond how a row starts (rule 21).

*What this withdraws in what is built and briefed.*

- The sixth pass's symbols made one for each concept the store reads (§23.4.5, part B: `symbol_for` at a declaration, in `bring_concept` for every word, at the class raise, in `define`; 110 symbols in the lesson, 101 of them for declared concepts). They come out. MTM's own nominations of symbols (`promote_identity`, `promote_candidates`) stay.
- Rule 10's sentence written by Claude in §23.4.4's review, "a concept that is declared and not nominated has its symbol made at its declaration", and the first step of what was left of round 4, "a symbol for every concept the store reads".
- The seventh pass, whose one task was to make the store's columns those one-member symbols with every value unchanged. It was told to stop, to leave the source as it found it, and to return its list of every writer and reader of the store's columns, which is wanted whatever the columns become.

*What a Sigma above order zero then reads* (Claude's reading of his sentences, with §19.98's "concepts are created from symbols and percepts via Not and Sigma"; put to him). A Sigma reads rows of a Pi, and the rows beneath a concept are of two kinds: basic percepts and symbols. Laid against what the store reads today (§23.4.5's measure):

| What reads | What it reads today | Under his two sentences |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The concept `words`, the grammar's arguments, and MTM's candidates | the order-zero concepts of the lesson's words (5 of the 8 things read in the lesson) | A kind whose objects are words reads the words' basic percepts, their rows, through the Not. It needs no symbol and no order-zero concept between. |
| The grammar's operator classes | the arguments, which are concepts (3 of the 8) | *The open case, below.* |
| A class that MTM raises from statements that share a side | classes, which are concepts (the gate's 3) | *The open case.* |

*The open case, put to him with an example.* A kind whose objects are themselves concepts: the operator class that ranges over the arguments `noun` and `adjective`, or the higher `cat` that ranges over what "Felix is a cat" and "Ciao is a cat" made. A Sigma reads rows, so there must be rows for it to read. His words of §19.87 have MTM make them: "MTM should be the place where that higher-order concept is created, by creating a higher order symbol over those two if not present". *Claude's first choice, as its reading of that:* the row is a symbol that MTM nominates when it recognizes the kind, and its constituents are what occurs together in each instance (in "Felix is a cat", Felix and cat), so the higher concept collects one symbol for each instance and not one symbol for each member concept. The other reading: one symbol whose single constituent is the member concept, made only at that moment and only because the kind needs it, which is the one-to-one form again and so is not taken.

*§19.83's "it connects to both lower rows"* (order one is n/2 connected to 3n/2) is read again in this light: the two rows beneath a concept of order one are the n basic percepts and the n/2 symbols of its own order. Claude had written "its own order's symbols and the n concepts of order zero".

### 19.102 Alec: a kind collects many symbols from every lower order; a symbol is a region of sameness; what the two epistemic levels of an order are for (2026-11-20)

His answer to §19.101's open case.

"For a kind whose members are themselves concepts (an operator class over arguments, or the higher cat), its Sigma reads symbols from all lower orders. It may be nominated by MTM, or implicitly occurring.

Lets clarify this a bit. Take the concept green things: it must collect elements from all orders, because both Felix and cats may be green. But it collects only from lower orders, so that it is at least well-defined (no sets of all sets). For it to collect just one symbol would make pi be the only fold, which is not correct: we must have lists of arbitrary things.

Consider also the symbol: should it represent just one concept? not necessarily: we might have two closely related concepts like "my dog" and "Voyager". They are actually the same object, so they will occur in the same conceptual space, but for most intents and purposes we should treat them the same. But we don't want to represent both with one vector, we want a region in semantic space. So the region specification for similarity is defined with the pi.

Is this clear? does it show how alternating epistemic levels within an order serve different functions?"

*It is clear, and it is decided* (rule 71, restated). Said back:

| Epistemic level | What it makes | Its fold | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pi | a *thing*: a basic percept at order zero, a symbol above | all of its constituents together | sameness. Its row is a region of the space beneath, and what falls in the region is treated as the one thing: "my dog" and "Voyager" are two concepts and one symbol. They keep their two vectors; the symbol is the region, not a vector that stands for both. A symbol may hold one concept or several. |
| Sigma | a *kind*: a concept | any of its members, a list | a list of arbitrary things. `green things` collects Felix and it collects cats, which are of different orders; it collects from every lower order and from no order at or above its own, so that it is well defined. A kind that could hold one symbol only would make the Pi the only fold. |

So the two levels of an order do two different things and neither can do the other's: the Pi says which are the same, by a region; the Sigma says which belong together, by a list. An order is one of each, and the next order's things are regions over this order's kinds.

*What it settles and what Claude had wrong.*

- *The open case of §19.101.* A kind whose members are concepts reads symbols, from every lower order, any number of them. It is nominated by MTM or occurs implicitly.
- *Claude's first choice there is withdrawn:* a symbol for each instance of a kind, with the member and the kind as its constituents (Felix and cat). A symbol's constituents are what is the same thing, not a member with its kind.
- *A symbol of one concept is not wrong in itself.* What was wrong (§19.101) was making one for every concept as a rule and addressing it as "the symbol of" that concept. A thing may be one concept, and may come to be several.
- *§19.83's "both lower rows"* stands as read in §19.101: a concept of order one reads the basic percepts and the symbols.

*Mine, built on unless he says otherwise:*

1. *What a Sigma above order zero reads* is rows of a Pi from every lower order: the basic percepts, and the symbols of its own order and below. A kind of words (`words`, the grammar's arguments over the lesson's words) has its entries on the words' basic percepts.
2. *When the thing a kind needs has no row yet.* MTM, nominating the kind, makes the member's symbol if none holds it (his §19.87: "by creating a higher order symbol over those two if not present"), and looks first for one that does ("check for an existing fit first"). It is made because the kind was recognized, by MTM, and not for every concept.
3. *How two concepts come to be one symbol.* MTM nominates it when it recognizes that they always occur together, or from a statement that two are the same ("Felix is my cat", rule 10); the second concept joins the first one's symbol as a constituent.
4. *The Pi's fold over a symbol's constituents is the product,* as for a basic percept over its parts: the symbol is present as far as all of them are. Since they are the same thing they are present together. *Put to him:* whether a symbol should also be present when only one of its concepts is evidenced (the region as "either"), which a product does not give.

### 19.103 Alec: symbols may be made liberally; a neighbourhood of identity (2026-11-20)

To the fourth point of §19.102, "Should a symbol also be present when only one of its concepts is evidenced?": "I think we can be liberal when creating symbols in that way, it still still defines a neighborhood of identity and enables us to reason over the concept (i.e. with other concepts)."

*Taken so* (rule 71; *Claude's reading of "in that way", said back to him*):

- *A symbol is present when any one of its concepts is evidenced.* The symbol of "my dog" and "Voyager" is there when either is. It is a neighbourhood of identity, and what falls anywhere in the neighbourhood is the thing. So the fold over a symbol's constituents is not their product. *Mine:* it is the Pi taken on the complements, one less the product of what each constituent lacks, the form the model already has for joining (rule 7's "Pi on the gaps"); with one constituent it is that constituent's own lanes. The product stays the fold of a basic percept over its parts and properties, which are all needed.
- *Symbols may be made liberally.* A symbol of one concept is no fault: it "still defines a neighborhood of identity", and it is what lets a concept be reasoned over with other concepts, since a kind collects things. What rule 71 rules out is not the making of such symbols but treating one as "the" symbol of a concept, one for one, with no room for a second concept to join it or for a concept to lie in two.

*What changes.* The ninth pass was sent the fold while it ran. §19.102's "the Pi's fold over a symbol's constituents is the product" is withdrawn. The removal of the sixth pass's symbols (§23.4.7, part A) stands, since those were made and addressed one for one; a later pass may make symbols more freely than "where a kind needs one", which is all the ninth pass makes.

*A consequence Claude notes, for round 5 or later:* a symbol and a kind over the same concepts now differ by what they are for and how they are folded and taught, and not by "all" against "any". A symbol's constituents are joined without weights, as the same thing; a kind's members are a weighted list through the Not, any of which may count for or against.

### 19.104 Alec: the fold of a symbol and the fold of a basic percept are to be one form (2026-11-20)

On §19.103's "a symbol's fold over its constituents is not their product. I have built it as the Pi on the complements": "But you say that the basic percept unites under a plain product. Please give a few examples of each, I think they need to be of the same form (for biological plausibility)."

**The examples he asked for.**

*A basic percept, the plain product over what it is made of.* The row of `cat` reads its parts c, a and t, each where it lies, and its properties:

| What is read | c | a | t | The row |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `cat` | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| `ca` and a mark read as a `t` at one half | 1 | 1 | .5 | .5 |
| `cab` | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |

In `cats` the row reads 1 for and, since the holder's added `s` is there, 1 against, and the Not gives nothing.

*A symbol as §19.103 had it, the Pi on the complements over its concepts.* The symbol of "my dog" and "Voyager":

| "my dog" | "Voyager" | One less the product of what each lacks |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| .8 | 0 | .8 |
| .8 | .5 | .9 |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |

**Why they came out as two forms, which was Claude's error.** In the first table the constituents are what the thing is made of, and all are needed. In the second Claude took the two *concepts that are the same thing* as the symbol's constituents. Those are alternatives, met one at a time, so a product over them could never be present, and Claude reached for the other fold. But what stands to a symbol as "my dog" and "Voyager" do is not c, a and t. It is two occurrences of `cat`, here and there, in this hand and that: they are not constituents of the row at all; they are what falls inside its region. So the difference was in what was counted as a constituent, and the fold should not have carried it.

**One form** (rule 71, restated; the complement fold of §19.103 is withdrawn, and the ninth pass was told so while it ran). A row of a Pi, at every order, is the plain product over its constituents, and its constituents are what always occurs together when the thing is there. What is the same thing is whatever falls in the row's region. A basic percept and a symbol are one class with one fold.

**What that leaves open, put to him.** If "my dog" and "Voyager" are not the symbol's constituents, what are? Two candidates, and they are different builds:

1. *Concepts that always occur with the thing,* read as activations, as a symbol's row reads concepts now (rule 10). The thing Voyager would have, say, the kinds dog and mine as constituents. "My dog" evidenced brings both, and the product is one. "Voyager" alone, heard as a name, brings them only as what is known of Voyager, which is expected and not evidenced.
2. *Coordinates of conceptual space,* so that the Pi above order zero reads the space of meanings as the first Pi reads the perceptual code: the row is a cone in semantic space and any concept whose meaning lies in it is the thing. This is the exact mirror of order zero, and it is what his words describe ("we want a region in semantic space. So the region specification for similarity is defined with the pi"; "identity/generalization on a hypercone"). It reverses two things the rules have: that a symbol's row reads concepts' lanes and no code (rules 9 and 10), and that likeness of codes pairs nothing (rule 16; his "no geometric influence" of 2026-11-15); and it would ask of the concepts' codes what rules 50 to 61 ask of the percepts', that one lie inside another only where it is meant.

*Claude's reading is that he means the second.* Nothing is built on either until he says: the ninth pass makes symbols of one constituent, read by the plain product, which is right under both.

### 19.105 Alec: a row's constituents are coordinates of the space beneath; a similarity class is a cone in a subspace (2026-11-20)

To §19.104's question: "The basic percepts constituents are coordinates of perceptual space or , and the symbols constituents are coordinates of conceptual space. I think. please confirm the reasoning: we are collecting members of a similarity class, and that class is defined as a conic region in similarity space, which may in fact be a subspace of that space (thus irrelevant details of members are removed by their variation in that subspace)."

**The reasoning holds, and here is why in the row's own arithmetic.** A row of a Pi is the product of its constituents' values, each raised to its weight, with weights at zero or above.

- *It is a region.* The row is high exactly where every coordinate it weighs is high. With the weights summing to one it is the weighted geometric mean of those coordinates, which scales with the size of what it reads; so "the row is at least this share of the input's size" depends on the input's direction alone, and the region is a cone.
- *It is a region of a subspace.* A coordinate with weight zero is raised to the power zero and is one whatever it holds, so the row does not see it. The region is bounded in the coordinates it weighs and runs free in all the others.
- *That is how irrelevant detail is removed.* A product needs every coordinate it weighs, so a coordinate on which the members differ cannot keep its weight: one member low on it would shut that member out. What can stay weighed is what all the members share. So generalizing over members is dropping the coordinates on which they vary, and the class is the cone over the coordinates they have in common. One precision on his sentence: the members vary in the coordinates the subspace leaves out, and are alike in the ones it keeps.
- *It is the same statement at both orders.* A basic percept is the cone over the coordinates of perceptual space that its occurrences share; a symbol is the cone over the coordinates of conceptual space that the concepts which are the same thing share. One class, one fold (§19.104).

**What it rests on, checked in the source.**

1. *At order zero it holds by construction.* A percept's code is built so that one code lies inside another only where the one form is a part of the other (rules 50 to 61), so "falls in the cone" is "holds these parts and properties". As built the first Pi's row reads its parts and its properties, each of which is a region of the code; with rule 61 that and "reads the code's coordinates" say the same thing.
2. *Conceptual space is nearer to this than Claude said in §19.104.* A concept's meaning is already held in coordinates at zero or above, in pairs of poles, and is placed by shared size and not by angle: a concept's place moves toward the coordinates of the contexts it occurs in (`MereologicalCodes.placement_step`, the meet-ratio objective), and two codes are compared by how much of one lies in the other (`IdentityRows.meet_ratios`). So concepts that occur in the same contexts come to share coordinates, which is what a cone over shared coordinates needs.

**Three things it asks for, each known from order zero.**

1. *The against side.* What falls in a cone includes whatever holds its coordinates and more: `cats` holds everything `cat` does. At order zero the row's against entries say so (rule 53). A symbol needs the same: what its nearest neighbours in conceptual space have that it has not.
2. *One meaning at a time.* If the meanings of all the concepts active in a sentence are joined before the symbols' Pi reads them, the join can cover a cone that none of them is in. That is the fault of §19.89 one order up (the concept of `alpha` lit by the letters of `beta` and `delta` together). The symbols' Pi reads the meaning at a place, as the first Pi reads a form where its run lies.
3. *No circle between codes and what reads them.* A concept's place is moved by the contexts it occurs in, and a symbol would now be read from places. The guard the model has ("codes never read a value computed from codes", 2026-10-20) has to be said again for this.

**What it changes in the rules** (rule 72, *his direction, "I think"; Claude's form of it, to be tried in tests before anything in the source*). A symbol's row reads coordinates of conceptual space and not the lanes of named concepts (rules 9 and 10 said the second); the likeness of codes now does pair something, but only through a symbol's cone (rule 16 said nothing; his "no geometric influence" of 2026-11-15 was about scores and moves, and is kept for those). Nothing of round 4's ninth pass is undone by it: a symbol of one concept read by the plain product is the cone about that one concept's own coordinates in the limit.

**The trial, in tests only.** On the lesson's model and on a small set of concepts known to be the same thing and known not to be: the row over the coordinates two same concepts share takes both in and keeps the others out; how many coordinates are shared after the lesson's placement; whether an against side is needed to keep out a concept that holds more; and what a join of two unrelated meanings lights.

### 19.106 Alec's answers to the questions left for item 1.7 (2026-11-20)

Asked "are there any remaining spec questions for 1.7?", Claude gave four that needed his decision and a list of its own readings. His answers, each under the question as it was put.

**1. May anything teach which bytes belong to a declared class such as `letter`?** "We can fix their membership, which makes their explicit representation dominate their implicit. But that makes the mind brittle; it might not learn greek letters or novel conceptual wholes, or its meaningful region might be wrong (if the concept cannot move)." *Taken:* they are not fixed. A declared class starts from what is declared and can be moved by what is learned, or the mind cannot learn a letter it was not told of. *What follows for what is built* (*mine*): the fifth pass's cut, which stops a concept's error at order zero from teaching the memberships (§23.4.4), was made because attention's table read a membership of .9999992 as "both" by an exact test of nothing. It stays only until round 6 removes that table; then the gradient is put back and the lesson measured over 12 runs with it. The reconstruction teaches the memberships meanwhile.

**2. The teacher of `intuit`'s map.** "I approve your choice: restore what you approved on 2026-11-12, the field that thought leaves, with the output's cost." *Decided* (rule 68): `intuit`'s map is taught by the field that thought leaves and by the cost of the output; omission teaches expectation alone.

**3. Growing the sparse Sigma by the penalty.** "Help me design implicit sigma and pi growth. MTM for explicit works well, our implicit methods are not working." *The design is §19.107.*

**4. Orders under the cone.** "A symbol's cone is tested only against concepts *at* its order, because the concepts at every order live in spaces with different geometries." *Decided* (rule 72). A symbol is a cone in the conceptual space of one order, and its constituents are coordinates of that one space; it never mixes concepts of two orders. A kind then collects symbols from every epistemic level below it (§19.102), which is how `green things` holds Felix and cats. *Claude's reading of "its order":* the order of the concepts the symbol is a cone over, since an order rises only at a Sigma (his word under the third reading below).

**On Claude's readings.**

- *"`words` and the grammar's arguments put their entries directly on the words' basic percepts."* "Technically this is wrong: basic percepts are events, or occurrences of words, because all of their constituent percepts occur at the same time, so there is no basis for abstraction into a noun. Can we make it one order higher without performance penalty?" *Withdrawn, and corrected* (rule 71). A basic percept is an occurrence. The word, over its occurrences, is its concept of order zero; the word as a thing is a symbol over that concept; and a kind of words, such as noun, collects those symbols. *On the cost, yes:* a symbol of one constituent has its concept's two values, so reading it is a lookup and not a product; the ninth pass was told while it ran, and returns the cost measured.
- *"Where a kind's member has no symbol, MTM makes one when it nominates the kind, after looking for one that already holds the member."* "Good." *Decided.*
- *"A kind of order k reads only things below order k."* "Use the term epistemic level, not order (which increases only with sigma). But OK." *Decided, in his terms:* a kind collects only from epistemic levels below its own. An order rises at a Sigma and nowhere else.
- *The cone's against side, one located meaning, no circle.* "Just to be clear, we are using an unsigned-weight PI on signed conceptual inputs. That means that the PI cannot change the sign, so it must allocate two lanes in order to operate on a given concept. Similarly, we are using an unsigned-weight Sigma on signed conceptual inputs from the NotLayer, so it does not need this doubling. The NotLayer operates over unsigned two channel symbols (or percepts) and yields signed outputs (possibly negated)." *Recorded as the types of the three steps* (rule 63):

  | Step | Its input | Its weights | Its output |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Pi | signed values of concepts, each given as two unsigned lanes, since a Pi cannot change a sign | unsigned | a thing on two unsigned lanes |
  | Not | a thing's two unsigned lanes | none | one signed value, the value or the not-value |
  | Sigma | signed values from the Not; no doubling | unsigned | a concept's one signed value |

- *The chooser's log (act, place, what it returned, in 8 slots).* "Please just document this, and track (for review in 1.6) which gradients are actually being used to help the chooser." *Decided:* rule 69 is documented and not built in item 1.7. Item 1.7 returns, with its last round's measurements, which costs' gradients reach each of the chooser's parameters over the lesson and how large each is; item 1.6 reviews it.
- *"A mereological or taxonomic link (depending on order)."* "No, I was thinking mereology is part-whole relation at the perceptual level which, when it occurs over symbols, becomes a taxonomy (because the sigma fold makes the concepts abstract). But you are right to point out that concepts (and percepts) live in a topological space, while symbols do not." *Corrected in the glossary:* mereology is part and whole among percepts; the same relation among symbols is taxonomy, because the Sigma's fold has made what they stand for abstract. Percepts and concepts live in spaces; symbols do not.
- *"The comparator gives distance in ticks."* "which somparator?" The one of his §19.91: "they will need a comparator to know how far back in history the concept they have recalled is". Rule 64 has it as a function of the present time and a concept's `.when`; "in ticks" was Claude's addition to say what it returns.
- *"Old checkpoints are refused, with no migration."* "OK". *Decided.*
- *"`transformChooser` should probably default to the network."* "more explanation necessary." The network that scores a walk's or a parse's next act has two forms, chosen by the key `transformChooser`. Set to `mlp` it is a small network with one hidden layer. Left out, it is a linear score: for each act, the inner product of the candidate with one learned vector for that act. A linear score weighs each thing it reads by itself; it cannot learn "after this act, when it returned nothing, do that", which is a conjunction of two things read, and so it could make no use of a log of the walk. Of the 44 configurations in `data/`, 10 set the key to `mlp` (the lesson's and the main ones among them) and 34 leave it out and get the linear score (the XOR, addition, grammar, image and memory fixtures). *Put to him again with that said:* whether the linear form is kept as the default, the network becomes the default, or the linear form goes so that there is one. Not changed.
