>    zero. At the second look the sum of absolute gradients at the request
>    was 0.00659, and every gradient at the query was zero. In an isolated
>    backward pass, scaling that query to 2% of its magnitude and applying
>    the same incoming gradient gave a nonzero query gradient. That isolates
>    the loss of sensitivity to the match. The scale was a diagnostic probe.
>
> 2. The ordinary corpus run does not teach the next-word request.
>
>    The 16-sentence corpus run through MathChainTraining.present supplied
>    no ReadingTargets on any of the 25 reading paths observed. The context
>    projection stayed exactly zero. On a subsequent reading of "This is
>    Felix.", all four looks asked only for the starting concept "words".
>    SentenceLooks.Looks.run lowers the activity of a word after it is
>    interpreted. Attention.draw_among selects the strongest remaining word
>    and draws randomly among exact ties. This can recover every word while
>    visiting the words out of order. The explicit reading_lesson path
>    supplies the next-word loss and replays the named target during training.
>    Its learned order must therefore be measured with that target removed.
>
> 3. The places test marks some correct readings as failures.
>
>    test/test_item17_places.py passes the length of the padded forms array
>    to AttentionLesson.in_order. That helper expects the accepted positions
>    to equal range(count). In the corpus fixture the live source positions
>    of "This is Felix." were [0, 2, 4, 5] in a 32-slot array. Reading those
>    four positions in precisely that order still fails this comparison.
>
>    I rescored an explicitly trained places fixture using interpreted
>    arrivals from Looks.source_orders() and the ordered source slots with
>    live spans. After training, one unforced evaluation gave 4 of 6
>    two-word sentences, 0 of 16 lesson sentences and 1 of 6 held-out
>    sentences in order. The existing helper scored zero in all three sets.
>    The corrected counts still show a failure to learn reliable order.
>
> Suggested next experiment
>
> Score interpreted arrivals against the live source slots for each sentence
> and batch row. Include a correct reading with gaps and padding, plus a
> reading of the same words with two arrivals swapped. With that measure in
> place, test the scale of the context query relative to the concept codes.
> Track the request and its gradient on the first two looks, then evaluate
> without a supplied reading on sentences containing the same words in
> different orders. This checks whether the location request can move after
> the first word and whether that movement predicts the next word in text.

*Checked by Claude:* point 3 is true in the source (`test_item17_places.in_order` passes the length of the padded forms to `AttentionLesson.in_order`, which wants the positions taken to equal `range(count)`). So every "0, 0, 0" that §23.6.6 to §23.6.12 report from the places' measure is in part this fault, and the counts of the lesson's script (0 to 2 sentences in order) measured a draw, since by point 2 that path teaches no next-word request. Points 1 and 2 are not reproduced by Claude. The bound of point 1 was Claude's first choice (§19.121), built in the eighth pass (§23.6.13).

Alec, asked whether the request should use the match both ways or the query be scaled: "I was thinking that the query would be activation of the concept \"words\" and an empty concept which could learn \"next\" over trained data." Then: "\"Next \" is not clear in my mind. But since we highlight \"words\" which will cause the salience to focus on the words we have learned, we might also have a cur for the .when focus, which we should be able to derive from a lit neuron and knowledge of the last attend .where. It would also help to have some memory of the full percept bank in order to know where to point the .where window of attention."

*What follows* (Claude; nothing is decided beyond his words):

- The query is a set of lit concepts, "words" among them, and not a free vector matched against every concept's code. So neither "the match both ways" nor "the query scaled" is built.
- Beside "words" there is a cue for the focus, derived from a lit concept and the `.where` of the last look. Today the last look's `.where` does not reach the next request (the context is given the surprise alone).
- The memory of the full percept bank exists: the sentence's field of percepts is made once and held (`PerceptBank`), and a word read is lowered in it.
- *To be tried in tests before anything is built* (the ninth pass): the cue as a concept that carries the `.where` of the word just read, each unread word scored by how near its `.where` is to it, with what is learned being the offset; the first word, which has no last look, by the learned start or a draw.

### 19.125 Alec: the tree being built is presented to `attend`, with the code and the `.where` of each word found (2026-11-22)

To Claude's question how attention should find the first word and move on (a learned start place on the `.where` as the next small trial), Alec: "A small trial on .where sounds appropriate. Codex has written diagnostic steps to suggestions.txt
My architectural idea would be to present the tree structure that we are building to the attend mechanism and perhaps the chooser in general, which stores the codes and .where of previous words as found (I don't think we are saving that information right now, just the stored words, so we would need to save  the .where that we provided for each look)."

Checked at `5364c905bc` (Claude):

- *He is right that it is not saved.* A look's decision keeps the index of the word taken (`Looks.decisions`: `index`, `slot`) and the walk keeps each taken word's key (`state.record`: `values` from `keys`). The `.where` of the word a look took is in the sentence's bank at the occurrences of its reading and is copied nowhere. The look's own request is not kept either.
- *What `attend` is given today:* the context's map of the last look's surprise (`context(surprise)`), and the learned start over concepts (`model.request_start`). Nothing of the tree, and nothing of the words found.
- *Codex's steps are in the checkout's `suggestions.txt`, not on GitHub* ("Finding the first word and remembering where to look next", 2026-11-22; copy at `scratch-1.7/suggestions_local_2026-11-22_first_word.txt`). Taken into the trial below, each as Codex put it:
  - a learned start on the `.where` for the first look, with first-word accuracy measured apart from what follows it: "Once all the words to the left have been read, the nearest unread word is already the next one. A better start could improve whole-sentence accuracy while leaving open whether attention can learn to move right."
  - the paired histories: in a sentence that repeats ("red cat red cat red"), two interpreted words are supplied and the third look is free. After the 2nd word then the 4th, the next to the right is the 5th; after the 4th then the 2nd, it is the 3rd. Both histories read the same words; only the most recent `.where` differs. A pair counts only if both free choices are right.
  - two versions of one small scorer on the pairs: the first with the STM's features available before the query, the second with those and the `.where` of the last interpreted occurrence.
  - for every choice, whether the intended word had a finite score ("is" sometimes scored -inf and could never be selected).
  - Codex's two observations, to be checked: STM already carries spatial intervals for its constituents, which composition merges into one; the attention projection reads detached inputs, so the reading-order cost gives the memory's writer no gradient by that path.
  The earlier "Suggested next experiment" (2026-11-21) is also taken in where the ninth pass did not build it: the scale of the query against the codes; the request and its gradient at the first two looks; sentences that hold the same words in other orders.

*Decided:* a trial in tests only, the tenth pass of round 6d (§22.6d). *Mine, to be shown by the trial and not assumed:* whether a request for one place tells the word at that place from its neighbours at all, since the `.where` codes of neighbouring words differ by about .01 on a wire (§19.121, 4; the cue's trial, §23.6.14).

### 19.126 Alec: a "first" concept held lit, a "next" concept lit after it, and the request in the input (2026-11-22)

Alec, after §19.125: "It will be sufficient to keep the unused node on and provide the request in the input, which will give opportunity for successor logic (which, if stored across LTM references, should give the basis for sequence learning).
So maybe we try one concept held lit as the "first" concept learner, and then light one that is the "next" context learner (we might not want these at low order). Enough info for a small test of a toy?"

Claude's reading, each part *mine* until he confirms it:

- *"The unused node"* is the empty concept of §19.124 (a concept with no definition, there to learn over trained data). It is kept lit; nothing else is built for it.
- *"The request in the input":* the request a look was given is part of the input of the next `attend`. So what a lit concept can learn is a map from the last request to the next one, which is a successor.
- *Two concepts.* "first" is lit while no word has been found, and what it learns is the request of the first look. "next" is lit after a word has been found, and what it learns is the successor: the next request from the last.
- *"Not at low order":* the two concepts are above order zero. The toy has no orders; where they would live in the model is left open.
- *"Stored across LTM references":* a successor learned once and kept by the references of LTM1 (`ref()`) would chain into a sequence. Not in the toy.
- *Open in the reading:* whether the request in the input is the request as given (over concepts) or as answered (the `.where` and code of the word the look returned, §19.125). The toy tries both.

*His correction, the same day:* ""Unused node one" meaning our current architecture, augmented with first/next and a memory of the what/where at the pi closest to the input that did the previous filtering." So Claude's first point was wrong: nothing is a separate empty concept. It is the architecture as it stands, with three additions: the "first" concept, the "next" concept, and a memory, at the first Pi (the Pi nearest the input), of the `.what` and the `.where` it selected at the previous look. That memory is the request "in the input": form B below (as answered), held where the filtering was done, and not the request as given over concepts. Form A stays in the toy only as the comparison.

*And then:* "A memory at the first Pi might be replaced with just the primed conceptual field which will carry that activity by wire (is that updated every attend?). Would it make sense for a chooser network to provide MLP input to each operator, such that they can have access to calculation on that surface but share a single network to do so? Or maybe they each share a linear layer on top of such?"

- *Is it updated every attend?* (Claude, at `5364c905bc`.) The conceptual field is: every look reads the sentence's bank anew through the first Pi and the Sigma (`SentenceLooks.perceive`), and the look's field is kept (`Looks.fields`). The next `attend` does not read it: its query is the context's map of the last surprise alone. The priming heat (`prime_seen`) has no call inside the looks; whether it moves at each `attend` is not verified and is asked of the tenth pass.
- *The toy gains form C:* the memory is the previous look's conceptual field, by wire, and nothing is kept at the first Pi. Compared with form B.
- *The chooser's network* (Claude's opinion, *for Alec*): his second form, one network shared by every operator over that surface with one linear read for each operator on top. The operators then learn one description of the surface and differ only in what they read from it, and an operator added later costs one linear read. The toy compares it with a read of its own for each concept.

*Decided:* a toy, in tests only, step 7 of the tenth pass.

### 19.127 Alec: the reading task is paired with "first, next*, end" on the output (2026-11-22)

Of the toy's two concepts, Alec: "Good, these two are provable sufficient, and invoking a read by flipping on a few neurons can be a method that we can generalize for learning different tasks." (`doc/FutureWork.md`, owed, after his answer on sequence learning over LTM.) Then: "To remove the intrusivity, I think we can pair the reading task with "first, next*, end" on the output."

Claude's reading, *mine* until he confirms it:

- *The intrusion* is the reading lesson's target: a cost that names the next word of the reading and replays it (`ReadingTargets`), laid on the looks from outside (§19.124, 2), as he said of the reconstruction cost ("That loss function gets intrusive", §19.121).
- *The pairing:* the output is produced by the same sequence, one "first", any number of "next", then "end". The cost is the output's own (the sentence reconstructed in its order), and the reading has no target of its own. The reading and the output share the two concepts, so what the output's cost teaches "first" and "next" is what the reading uses.
- *"end"* is a third concept, lit when nothing is left; it is where the sequence stops, in place of a count.

*Decided:* tried in the toy, step 8 of the tenth pass.

### 19.128 Alec: the concepts are not taught explicitly; back to reading without comprehension; an object counting task (2026-11-22)

After §19.127, Alec: "We shouldn't have to teach the concepts explicitly. Let go back to reading without comprehension if the toy proves it can work, and make sure to introduce an object counting task as 1,2,3,4 counting word on the output."

- *Decided:* "first", "next" and "end" are not given as named concepts with a lesson each. Claude's reading (*mine*): one unused concept is lit for a task, and what it does at the first look, at a later look and at the end is learned from the output's cost and from what the memory holds (nothing; a word; nothing left). The three names describe what is learned and are in no source.
- *Decided:* if the toy shows it works, the item goes back to reading without comprehension (stage one: the sentence read and reproduced, no idea asked of it) with the looks on, taught by the output alone.
- *Decided:* an object counting task. The input holds objects; the output is the counting words "1", "2", "3", "4", one for each object, in order. Numerals are opaque words and the successor is the one relation (his rule for math). It is a second task for the same mechanism, with a concept of its own lit. Tried in the toy (step 9 of the tenth pass) and entered in item 1.6's plan.

### 19.129 Alec's answers to the tenth pass: build it in the model; a concept is lit by the input or by the output, never directly (2026-11-22)

Of the priming, which is written once when a sentence opens and not inside the looks (§23.6.16): "I think we can and do want to spread activation for the look, but we do not want to do the big N:N step". *Decided:* at each look the look's field spreads activation (`ConceptSpread.spread`), and the next `attend` reads the field so spread. The N:N map of the expectation is not run for it.

To Claude's six questions (§23.6.16), each answer whole:

1. *Build it in the model?* "yes, build it, but lets generalize the "lighting the concept" idea, and somehow bake it into the model such that it can be done via input or output. You say that "the models own reading" still fails, and that is ultimately what we want to fix."
2. *The memory is the last look's conceptual field by wire?* "Agreed."
3. *A short `.where` rung of 16 to 32 addresses?* "If necessary"
4. *A successor over places?* "OK, just one concept. This is not something that we want to dictate, in general, it is too model-intrusive."
5. *Two tasks together, or in the curriculum's order?* "I think multiple external tasks would have a bearing on, and perhaps triangulate, the internal conceptual solution that we do not want to light up directly."
6. *Past "4", left to item 1.6?* "No, finish."

Claude's reading, each part *mine* until he confirms it:

- *No concept is lit by a switch.* The toy lit an unused concept by hand for each task. In the model nothing does that. A concept is lit by the model's own paths: by the input (a word of the input lights its concept by the ordinary read, and the sentence's opened field holds it for every look), or by the output (the word last said lights its concept, which the next `attend` reads). So a task is given from outside in one of two ways: a word in the input, or the beginning of the output. What `attend` reads is the conceptual field, whatever lit it.
- *The inner solution is not named and not lit.* How to look (take the leftmost unread, stop when nothing is left) is learned inside the one network every task shares, and the tasks, taught together, are what shape it (the toy: taught together, the two concepts' rows come out alike and light the same units). No lesson is given to a concept, no reading target, no reading from a drawn word, and no successor over places (4).
- *"Finish"* (6): counting is finished in this item and in the model, with counting words past "4". How far the lesson's counting words go is Claude's (to "9"); what the model says past the last word taught is reported and nothing is built for it.
- *The rung* (3) is added only if the model's reading cannot tell neighbours without it, and then as a key of `data/model.xml`.

*His correction of that reading, the same day:* "I just mean we should not be setting the activation of concepts directly; they should always come from input and output. Its bad enough that we are creating some at init. as for META concepts. So teach reading and counting over words, as separate output tasks, over the same input sentences on the same model and weights: lets see if that is sufficient."

- *Decided:* the rule is only that no activation of a concept is set directly; every activation comes from the input or from the output. (Concepts made at the start, as the meta concepts are, he counts as a cost already paid and not as a model to follow.)
- *Decided:* counting is over the words of a sentence, not over a row of objects. The two tasks have the same input sentences, the same model and the same weights, and differ only in the output asked: the sentence itself, or one counting word for each of its words. No word is added to the input to name the task (Claude's "a word of the input that comes with the task" is withdrawn).
- *Decided:* it is a trial of sufficiency ("lets see if that is sufficient"): nothing more is built to tell the tasks apart until this has been measured.
- *Mine:* since the inputs are the same, at evaluation a task can only be given by the output: its first word supplied. What the model says with nothing supplied is reported too.

Rule 80 (§21). *The eleventh pass* (§22.6d) builds it.

### 19.130 Alec: words first until learned, then reading over them, then the grammar one rule at a time; lean on the assessment (2026-11-22)

Alec, while the eleventh pass was building: "Also, maybe we want to reliable teach reading all of the words until they are learned, and then reading over them, and then the grammar (with rules one at a time). We have talked about internal and external forms of this harness, and i think we agreed it should be an external evaluation tool, but perhaps we can lean on that more heavily (e.g. when answering questions in chat) to make sure the model can do all of the required sub-goals (as we jave just been enumerating: outputting words, counting, reading, ...)"

- *What exists* (Claude): the external tool is the assessment (`bin/Assessment.py`, `bin/AssessmentProbe.py`, `data/assessment/known_probe.json`; `doc/plans/2026-11-15-assessment.md`). It is read-only, has a ladder of nine rungs from one word to "the fast cat ran quickly", and a test may name its rung and report "not ready". Its first rung's lesson, reading every word in order, was decided then ("Teach it first") and is what the eleventh pass rebuilds. `test/attention_curriculum_gates.py` holds a second ladder (reading two, reading four, identities, noun phrase, noun and verb, relations).
- *The order of teaching* (taken into the eleventh pass, step 4): each word alone until every word is said back; then sentences read over those words, with counting; a stage is left when its measure passes and not after a count of presentations. The grammar, one rule at a time, follows in the pass after.
- *Proposed, mine, for the pass after the eleventh:* the assessment's ladder gains rungs below its first, one for each sub-goal enumerated here, each with its own measure and each gating the next: (1) a word said back; (2) a sentence read in order and stopped; (3) its words counted; then (4 on) the grammar's rules one at a time, a rung for each rule, on the nine sentences it has. The two ladders become one. (A check in chat, proposed here, is withdrawn below.) It stays outside the model: it reads, and it changes no weight.

*His correction, the same day:* "I don't mean "in the context of a chat", that is too late for learning.

I mean that before we test understanding and identity, as we are now doing, we should qualify the model that we are testing with some assessment grade. They can be numeric, in a list, maybe corresponding to the approximate age in a human child at which they are learned, in years at a few decimal digits of precision."

- *Withdrawn:* Claude's check in chat.
- *Decided:* a model is qualified by the assessment before understanding and identity are tested on it. Each sub-goal has a number, in one list (he first said "assessment grade"; the word is *age*, below); the number is about the age in years at which a child learns it, to a few decimals.
- *Mine, a first list for his correction* (the ages are from memory of the usual milestones and were not looked up; the model's "reading" is taking the words of a sentence in order, which is nearer to a child's hearing and saying back than to literacy):

| Age (years) | Sub-goal | Measure (the assessment's) |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 0.70 | A word kept when it is out of the look (object permanence) | the ladder's rung "one word" |
| 1.00 | A word said back | each word alone in, the word out |
| 1.50 | Twenty words said back | the rung "twenty words" |
| 1.75 | Two words taken in order and said back | two-word sentences read in order and stopped |
| 2.00 | A thing named | "This is Felix."; the rung "Felix" |
| 2.25 | A noun and a verb | the rung "Felix ran" |
| 2.50 | A sentence of three to five words taken in order and stopped | the lesson's sentences, and held out |
| 2.75 | A determiner | the rung "the cat ran" |
| 3.00 | The counting words said in order, to "4" | counting over the words of a sentence |
| 3.25 | An adjective; a "what" question answered | the rung "the fast cat ran"; `identities` |
| 3.50 | A pronoun | the rung "he ran" |
| 4.00 | Each thing counted once, to "9" | counting, each word looked at once |
| 4.25 | An adverb | the rungs "Felix ran quickly", "the fast cat ran quickly" |
| 4.50 | Relations | `relations` ("is on", "bigger than") |

- *Mine:* a model's age is the greatest age of the list with every age below it passed, and the list of what passed is kept beside it. A test of understanding or identity names the age it needs; on a model below it the test reports "not qualified at age x" in place of a failure of its own. Built in the pass after the eleventh, in `bin/Assessment.py`, the two ladders made one.

*The term, and where the number is kept* (Alec, the same day): "Terminology change: A model’s age is determined by the assessment, not "grade"
The age can be a parameter of the model (and XML), read/written by the assessment, and which can be used by that tool to ensure that a test is qualified to run against the model (by asking for a specific mental age)."

- *Decided:* the word is *age* (a model's mental age), and "grade" is not used. The list above is a list of ages.
- *Decided:* the age is a parameter of the model and of its XML. The assessment determines it, writes it and reads it. A test asks the assessment for a mental age, and the assessment says whether the model is qualified for the test.
- *The chart:* "This mandates a chart called ModelAge somewhere in the doc/*.md that says what tasks have to be learned in order to qualify a certain mental age." (Alec, the same day.) It is `doc/ModelAge.md`, and the list above is its first form; the chart is kept there from now on, and the assessment's list is made to agree with it.
- *Mine, for the build:* a key `age` with its default (0) in `data/model.xml`; the number kept with the model's saved state, so that it goes with the weights it was measured on; `Assessment.py` the only writer. A model whose weights have changed since its age was written is assessed again before a test is qualified on it.

### 19.131 Alec: the chart is checked and widened; counting on request runs a loop in LTM (2026-11-22)

Alec: "Yes, please check them, and add detail to the chart even if all of it does not currently correspond to particular tests, since it might inform subgoals that will help us to break down a subsequent task.

One task besides reading is counting with no change in the input stimulus: "Please count from one to 15" should run a multi-step behavioral loop in LTM (since LTM is capable of storing outputs directly as one of its episodic memories)."

- *The chart is checked* (Claude, by search, 2026-11-22) and rewritten in `doc/ModelAge.md` with a basis for each row (sourced, or estimate) and rows that have no test yet. Several of Claude's first ages were too young: a thing named in a sentence with "is" moves from 2.00 to 2.75 (the copula is the seventh of Brown's morphemes, 27 to 39 months); a determiner from 2.75 to 3.00 (articles, 28 to 46 months); twenty words from 1.50 to 1.70; a sentence of five or six words to 4.00; four unrelated words said back in order is 5.00 (a forward span of about four items at 5 years), which is the curriculum's `reading_four`. Ages for the number-knower levels and for adverbs and comparatives were not found and stay estimates.
- *Decided:* a third task, counting on request. The input ("Please count from one to 15") does not change while the count goes on, so no look can say what comes next. Each counting word said is stored in LTM as an episode (LTM stores an output directly), and the next is recalled from it: a loop of several steps that runs in LTM.
- *Mine, how the loop would run on what is decided:* the LTM query is the match of the top of STM and the top result is pushed (§19.86). With the word last said on top, the result is the episode that followed it when the count was taught, and pushing it says the next word. The pairs of the count share sides ("1" then "2", "2" then "3"), which is where MTM makes a higher symbol (§19.87). The loop ends at the word named in the request, or where LTM returns nothing (rule 48). *To be checked in the source before it is specified:* that an output is written to LTM as an episode with its predecessor, and that the query can be made from an output and not only from an input.
- It is in the chart at 5.00 (an estimate). It is not in the eleventh pass.

### 19.132 Alec: `.what` and `.where` may be muxed at the basic percept as the modalities are; the `.where` is one space of three dimensions for every model (2026-11-22)

Alec, while the de-muxed way back was being built: "By the way, .what and .where might be muxed together at the basic percept just as different modalities (such as words and numbers) mux together. That would cause all percepts to live in a common (3d) perceptual space, even if some were of reduced rank (e.g., the location of smell might be considered as a point at the nose)."

- *Not decided* ("might"). Recorded as a direction.
- *What it would change* (Claude): today each modality has its own perceptual space with its own `.where` axes (§ of 2026-11-13, "per-modality `.where` axes"), and a basic percept's row keeps its `.where` and `.when` as learned entries beside its `.what` code (rule 62; §19.115, "where and when muxed before the product"). On his thought the `.where` would be one more thing muxed into the percept in the way a second modality is, and every percept of every modality would have a place in one space of three dimensions; a modality with no extent has a place of reduced rank (a point).
- *What it would give:* one mux and one de-mux for modalities and for `.what`, `.where` and `.when` alike, so that the way back of rule 79 separates them by the mechanism that separates words from numbers; and a common space in which a word, a number and a felt thing can be at the same place, which item 1.6's felt world (three axes) needs.
- *For the twelfth pass:* nothing is built for it. The pass says whether the source's separation of modalities (`InputSpace/demuxed`) and its separation of `.what` from `.where` on the way back are, or could be, one mechanism.
- *For item 1.6:* taken up there with the number modality.

*Decided, the same day.* To Claude's estimate of the cost (three axes at the two periods of today: 12 wires for 4, a concept 144 wide for 136, about 6% more; the place match per axis, three times today's and not its cube), Alec: "NB: we are treating numbers as felt things.

I would like to see .where as a 3D space for all models, it simplifies things. I am not convinced that we need 4 elements per dim as opposed to 3, but if they are only bf16 that's not too bad."

- *Decided:* the `.where` is a space of three dimensions for every model. A modality with no extent on an axis has a place of reduced rank on it (text lies on one axis). The per-modality `.where` axes of 2026-11-13 give way to it.
- *Noted:* numbers are felt things (Claude had written "a word, a number and a felt thing" as three).
- *Open, his doubt:* whether an axis needs four elements or three. It is measured before it is chosen (twelfth pass, d): the margin between neighbouring places with four elements for an axis (two periods, as today), and with three in the forms that fit (say which). Until then an axis keeps four.
- *The type:* the elements are of the model's type and are BF16 when the whole model is (`MODEL_AMP`); no narrower type of their own.
- *Mine, for the build:* the place code and its match are kept for each axis apart (one table for an axis, a place the three results together), so that three dimensions cost three matches; the number of axes a key of `data/model.xml`.

*What lies on which axes, and what a number is* (Alec, the same day): "Text will be 1D: zeros for dim 2 and 3.
The perception of intensity (feelings) can be 1,2, or 3D.
Images will generally be intensity, so zeros for dim 3. The can in principle be 1D
Volumes will be no different than 3D images.

Numbers are higher-order, so symbolic (they are pure forms, and do not have a perceptual representation). So in the tests where we had been talking about "one is above two", it should be seen as a shorthand for "the pixel value 1 (at x1,y1,z1) is above the pixel value 2 (at x2,y2,z2)": we are referring to image data. We can continue to refer to shapes in feeling space as level sets to teach basic geometry."

- *Decided:* text is on one axis, with zeros on the second and third (Claude's "at one point" is zeros).
- *Decided:* intensity, which is feeling, is perceived on one, two or three axes. An image is intensity, generally on two axes with zeros on the third, and may be on one. A volume is an image on three.
- *Decided, and it corrects the note above:* a number is not a felt thing. It is of a higher order and symbolic: a pure form with no perceptual representation. What is felt is the intensity. "One is above two" in a test is shorthand for "the pixel value 1 (at x1, y1, z1) is above the pixel value 2 (at x2, y2, z2)", and it speaks of image data.
- *Decided:* shapes in the space of feeling are level sets, and basic geometry is taught on them.

### 19.133 Alec: the concept is the concatenation of `.what`, `.where` and `.when`; reconstruction inverts it and does not depend on attention (2026-11-22)

To two sentences of Claude's reading of "The .where continues to be muxed on its way to conceptual space and demuxed to determine where percepts are located", Alec, each answer whole:

1. Of "an occurrence's `.where` travels muxed with it, as wires of what is carried, all the way up into conceptual space": "just as before, the .what, .where, and .when are concatenated to form the concept from the basic level percept that contains those separately. This process is inverted to project .what onto the codebook and the .where on the cerebellum (is that where the 3D space is stored for all modalities?)"
2. Of "the place is not decoded from which place concepts happen to be lit, and it is not something a word's row learns": "We had been stimulating concepts, finding their sensitivity on the input, and using that to select the percepts that are let in via attention. I assume that will still happen in attend(), but the conceptual activation should be driven by input or state. But the reconstruction, which does not depend on attention, will take the input back though the perceptual inverse and to a basic percept which can be disassembled and used to select the relevant mereological features over parts and wholes and the .where over the spatial parameter (are we still calling it the cerebellum?)"

*Decided:*

- The basic percept holds its `.what`, its `.where` and its `.when` apart. The concept is made from it by concatenating the three. Nothing new: "just as before".
- Reconstruction is the inverse of that and does not depend on attention. The input is taken back through the perceptual inverse to a basic percept; the percept is taken apart; its `.what` selects the features of parts and wholes (the percept codebook), and its `.where` selects over the spatial parameter.
- `attend` is a different thing and stays: concepts are stimulated, their sensitivity on the input is found, and that selects the percepts let in. The conceptual activation it starts from is driven by the input or by state, never set (§19.129).

*His two questions, answered from the source* (Claude, at `b0e14a35c7`):

- *"Is that where the 3D space is stored for all modalities?"* There is one store of places for every modality and every space, `WhereRegistry` (`bin/WhereRegistry.py`): one row of `.where` wires for each address (`code`), which is the spatial parameter. But it is one line of addresses cut into named ranges (the input, the parts, the wholes, the conceptual slots), and a modality is told from another by its range, not by a place in a common space. So: one store, yes; of three dimensions, no, not yet (§19.132, the twelfth pass's item f).
- *It is not learned today.* `WhereRegistry.code` is the sinusoid's code of each address. It takes a gradient and is in no optimizer ("nothing of it is learned or written as a state", its own comment). What is learned of a place is a row's entries on the `.where` wires (`PlaceEntries`, §19.120). So a cost that finds a percept at a wrong place can teach the rows that read places and cannot move the places. *For Alec:* whether the spatial parameter itself is to be learned.
- *"Are we still calling it the cerebellum?"* No name in the source says cerebellum; the source says `WhereRegistry`, and one sentence of `doc/BasicModel.md` says "In humans, perceptual space projects onto a 3D cerebellar subspace before symbolic encoding" (his, 2026-11-20). *For Alec:* the name. Until he says, the spec writes "the spatial parameter (`WhereRegistry.code`)".

*Decided, the same day* (Alec): "so we need an NN.param called cerebellum which is the 3D space filled with sinusoids that is copied (muxed) into the basic percepts, and demuxed to create the location for the associated vector in the percept codebook.

The spatial parameter should be fixed, we had this exact conversation before and said it should be an SOM if that is not too difficult (although we can leave that for future work since there is no need at this point for a cortical remapping)"

- *The name:* the spatial parameter is the *cerebellum*: one `nn.Parameter` of that name, the space of three dimensions filled with sinusoids. `WhereRegistry.code` becomes it, in the pass that makes the `.where` three-dimensional (§19.132, f).
- *What it does:* its code at a place is copied (muxed) into the basic percept at that place; on the way back the percept's `.where` is separated and matched against it, which gives the place of the vector the `.what` selected in the percept codebook.
- *It is fixed.* Nothing of it is learned: it takes a gradient, as today, so that a salience carried down reaches its rows, and it is in no optimizer. What a cost at a wrong place teaches is the rows that read places. Claude's question whether it should be learned had been answered before (§19.121, 2: the self-organizing map, future work) and should not have been asked again.
- *Future work, as already entered in `doc/FutureWork.md`:* a self-organizing map under it, "if that is not too difficult"; not now, "since there is no need at this point for a cortical remapping".

*The name changed, the same day.* Alec had asked a question of the brain and not of the source: "but I was asking if the cerebellum is in fact where 3D space is represented by the human brain, or if the hippocampus is largely responsible for that." Claude's answer, from memory and not looked up: the map of where things are is the hippocampal formation's (place cells in the hippocampus, grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex, tuned in three dimensions in flying bats); space relative to the body is the posterior parietal cortex's; the senses share one aligned map in the superior colliculus; the cerebellum supports the map (the vestibular part computes the head's orientation in three dimensions, and its learning keeps place cells stable) and does not hold it. The fixed sinusoid code at several periods is nearest to the grid cells, a periodic code for place at several scales, and the rows that read the `.where` are nearest to place cells. Alec: "lets call it the grid."

- *Decided:* the spatial parameter is the *grid*: one `nn.Parameter` named `grid`. Everything said of the cerebellum above is said of the grid; the word cerebellum is not used for it.
- *Noted for the rung* (§19.129, 3; his doubt of three or four elements): grid cells come in several modules whose spacing grows by a ratio of about 1.4 to 1.7, where the model has two periods at a ratio of 32.

## 20. The prototype of the looks, in tests only (Claude, standing in for Codex, 2026-11-18)

This returns the text of §19.47, as amended by §19.48 and §19.49. No file of `bin/` is changed and no existing test; nothing is wired into the model. It decides nothing.

### 20.1 The files (Claude, standing in for Codex, 2026-11-18)

- `test/looks_prototype.py`. The bank of a sentence (rule 33): each byte's row in a what codebook of the lesson's bytes, its place and that place's code from `Spaces.WhereEncoding` (the constant sinusoid, both rungs, capacity 4096), and the stem's token it belongs to (runs of letters, each mark on its own). The first layer (rule 2 of §19.21): rows are products over a token's memberships, `z = exp(W log clamp(m, ε, 1))`, weights at zero or more. A word row has weight on its letters' codebook rows (the count of each); the fixed word whole has weight one on every byte of the token being a letter; a place row has weight on both unsigned lanes of the token's place code, `k·c` on the code `c` and `k·(1 − c)` on its complement, so it peaks at the place and its radius narrows as `k` grows. The Sigma (rule 3): each concept is `tanh` of a weight times its row; the meta concept "word" is one row over the word concepts. The pullback (rule 36): the share of a byte is its activity times the derivative of the asked concepts by it, by the transposes of the same matrices with the local derivatives kept from the way up, and by the framework's backward. The two domains (§19.48, answer 2): the asked word, whole and meta rows give each byte its what match (its share, capped at one); the asked place rows, read at each byte's place, give its where match; the look's activity is their product. The returned set (rule 37) is the way up again on that activity; `interpret` takes the most active word concept, exactly. Also the fallback, the sinusoid profile and the trial of reading in order.
- `test/looks_prototype_report.py`, which prints every table below.
- `test/test_item17_looks_prototype.py`, nine tests of the claims below (9 passed, 3.9 s).

Three choices that the rules do not make were needed to run it; each is reported against its alternative below. (1) The Sigma is passed in the pullback by its slope (rule 36 as written) or by its weights alone. (2) A token's membership of a codebook row is the greatest of its copies, and in the pullback every copy at that greatest value takes the whole derivative (the framework's `amax` splits it among the copies). (3) The share becomes the look's activity capped at full presence, `min(1, share)`.

### 20.2 The pullback by the transposes is the framework's backward (Claude, standing in for Codex, 2026-11-18)

On the sixteen sentences, at full activity and at three random activities, for four requests:

| Sigma passed by | Comparisons | Largest difference |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| its slope | 256 | 2.8e-17 |
| its weights | 256 | 0.0 |

They agree once both use the same local derivatives. Out of the box they did not, for two reasons. `PiLayer2` (as `clamp(m, ε, 1)`) passes **no gradient at a membership of exactly one** in this torch (2.15): `PiLayer2(3, 3)` at `m = 1` gives a gradient of 0, and at `m = 0.999` about 1.01. A word wholly present stands exactly there, so the framework's backward through the Pi returns no share for it. The prototype clamps only the floor (an activity here never exceeds one). And the framework's `amax` splits a repeated letter's derivative between its copies, so `that` came back at a quarter.

The word meant: for a word, the sentence's last word; for the place, the word at token 1; for the meta concept with a place, the word at token 2. Place rows at concentration 200, applied inside the products. "Projection" is the weights alone: each byte whose letter is in an asked row.

| Request | Sigma passed by | Place read at | Taken as meant, first of equals | Taken as meant, largest of equals | Taken with a tie | Returned on "This is Felix." (token: word concepts at 0.5 or more) | Projection on "This is Felix." |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| the meta concept | slope | — | — | — | 0 of 16 | nothing | 0:This 1:is 2:Felix |
| the meta concept | weights | — | — | — | 16 of 16 | 0:This/is 1:is 2:Felix | 0:This 1:is 2:Felix |
| a word's concept | weights | — | 10 of 16 | 14 of 16 | 6 of 16 | 2:Felix | 0:This 1:is 2:Felix |
| the fixed word whole | weights | — | — | — | 16 of 16 | 0:This/is 1:is 2:Felix | 0:This 1:is 2:Felix |
| an absent word (`dog`) | weights | — | 16 of 16 | 16 of 16 | 0 of 16 | nothing | nothing (on "Who is here?", `Who` by its `o`) |
| a place | — | each byte | 16 of 16 | 16 of 16 | 0 of 16 | 1:is | all tokens |

What comes back is what was asked for and is present: an absent word returns nothing in all sixteen, where the weights alone let a word in on one shared letter. The meta concept returns every word, and with a place read at the token and the largest of equals taken, the word at the place in all sixteen, as §19.49 expects. The ties are the containment of §20.4.

### 20.4 Cost, and what the binding by token does and does not prevent (Claude, standing in for Codex, 2026-11-18)

| One way up | The pullback | One look (the pullback and the way up again) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 478 | 600 | 1,078 |

Multiply-adds per sentence, the mean over the sixteen, counted from the shapes (14 word rows, 20 codebook rows, 4 tokens). A look costs about 2.3 ways up, once for a request and not once for each candidate.

| Sentence | Request | Returned | Taken |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "Fe li x is here." (every letter of Felix, in three tokens) | Felix | nothing | nothing |
| "xileF is here." (the same letters in another order) | Felix | 0:Felix | Felix at token 0 |
| "This is Felix." | is | 0:is 1:is | is at token 0, tied with is at token 1 |
| "What is that?" | that | 0:that 2:that | that at token 0, tied with that at token 2 (`What` holds t, h and a) |

The binding by token stops letters spread over tokens. It does not see order inside a token: an anagram is the word, and a word whose letters are all in a longer token (`is` in `This`, `here` in `there`, `that` in `What`) is wholly present there. A product row is a test of containment, not of equality.

### 20.5 Dimming by the asking row (Claude, standing in for Codex, 2026-11-18)

The meta concept with a place at token 2 (`Felix`, first byte 8) on "This is Felix.": the most active word concept at each token as the place row's concentration narrows it, with the where match read at each byte's own place or at its token's first place, and applied inside the products or once to a token's reading.

| Concentration | Read at | Applied | This (token 0) | is (token 1) | Felix (token 2) | Taken |
| ---: | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 12.5 | each byte | inside | 0.932 | 0.991 | 0.984 | is |
| 12.5 | the token | inside | 0.255 | 0.989 | 0.995 | Felix |
| 12.5 | each byte | once | 0.293 | 0.924 | 0.995 | Felix |
| 50 | each byte | inside | 0.285 | 0.962 | 0.853 | is |
| 50 | the token | inside | 0.000 | 0.931 | 0.995 | Felix |
| 200 | each byte | inside | 0.000 | 0.506 | 0.096 | is |
| 200 | the token | inside | 0.000 | 0.277 | 0.995 | Felix |
| 200 | each byte | once | 0.000 | 0.307 | 0.995 | Felix |
| 800 | each byte | inside | 0.000 | 0.004 | 0.000 | is |
| 800 | the token | inside | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.995 | Felix |
| 3,200 | each byte | inside | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | nothing |
| 3,200 | the token | inside | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.995 | Felix |

(The full table, with "once" at the token's place too, is printed by the report; "once" at either place takes Felix at every concentration.) Read at each byte's own place, the dimming cuts the word that was asked for: a place's code holds its start and not its end, so the word's later letters lie away from the place and are dimmed, inside the product, once each. A short word near the place then wins, and at 3,200 nothing is left. Read at the token's first place, or applied once to the token's reading, the word at the place is taken at every concentration, and the other tokens fall from about 0.9 to nothing as the cone narrows. The row's value at its own place, its magnitude, falls as `exp(−k·H)` (H the entropy of its code); the Pi may not raise it (its bias is at zero or below), so the prototype gives the Sigma's weight on a place row the inverse of the row's magnitude.

### 20.6 The where sinusoid as a coordinate (Claude, standing in for Codex, 2026-11-18)

A place row at byte 200, concentration 200: its reading at a distance, over its reading at the place.

| Capacity | Rung | +1 | +2 | +4 | +8 | +64 | +128 | +255 | +256 | +512 | +4096 |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4096 | long | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.998 | 0.993 | 0.625 | 0.158 | 0.001 | 0.001 | 0.000 | 0.000 |
| 4096 | short | 0.888 | 0.627 | 0.162 | 0.001 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.884 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| 4096 | both | 0.888 | 0.627 | 0.162 | 0.001 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.001 | 0.001 | 0.000 | 0.000 |
| 64 | both | 0.788 | 0.389 | 0.024 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.783 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 |

At capacity 4096 the long rung's period is 8,192 bytes and the short rung's 256. Within a sentence the long rung separates nothing (0.998 four bytes away); the short rung does all of it, and alone it lets in every place a multiple of 256 bytes away, which the long rung then removes. At capacity 64 `WhereEncoding` gives both rungs the same period of 256, and nothing removes the repeats. At concentration 200 a place four bytes away reads 0.16 and one byte away 0.89; the words of a sentence begin three to six bytes apart.

It agrees with the returned sets of §20.3 wherever one word is at the place. It needs no pullback; it also needs no request, so nothing in it can be taught to ask.

### 20.8 Reading in order, taught on the request alone (Claude, standing in for Codex, 2026-11-18)

Each look asks for the meta concept and a place: the first at the sentence's start, each later one at the end of the word read last plus an offset. Only the offset is taught, by the gradient of a loss that asks the next word to be the most active, through the pullback, the place code (made continuous) and the way up. It starts at −3, inside the word just read.

| Steps | Offset | Sentences read wholly in order |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | −3.00 | 0 of 16 |
| 20 | 0.83 | 16 of 16 |
| 150 | 1.07 | 16 of 16 |

It learns to step one byte past the word read, onto the space before the next word, and then reads all sixteen in order. What was taught is one number shared by all sentences; nothing about which concepts to ask for was taught, and no done mark was used.

### 20.9 What surprised me (Claude, standing in for Codex, 2026-11-18)

1. *A saturated Sigma gives its strongest token almost nothing.* With the meta concept pulled back by the Sigma's slope, the token holding two whole words (`This`, and `is` inside it) gets about 1/300 of the share of a token holding one, and at full presence nothing is returned at all. The derivative is smallest where the concept is most lit. Passed by its weights, every letter of a present word has a share of at least one.
2. *The framework's backward through `PiLayer2` is zero at full membership* (§20.2). Rule 36's default, the transposes with the local derivatives kept, avoids it only if the derivative at the ceiling is defined to pass.
3. *A product row is containment.* Ties at the full value are the rule, not the exception: in every sentence for the meta concept and the whole, and in 6 of 16 for a single word. The largest of equals (§19.30) settles all but `that` inside `What`.
4. *The asked word is cut by its own place.* Dimming at each byte's place, inside the product, favours a short word beside the place over the word at it (§20.5).
5. *The long rung does nothing inside a sentence,* and at the small capacity the two rungs are one.

### 20.10 What I would change in rules 33 to 42 (Claude, standing in for Codex, 2026-11-18)

Each is *mine*, for Alec to take or not.

- **Rule 34.** Say how a share becomes the look's activity. *Default:* the share capped at full presence; a byte shared by two asked rows is not counted twice.
- **Rule 36.** The pullback passes the Pi by its product's derivative and the Sigma by its weights, not its slope; the greatest of a token's copies of a letter is a selection, every copy at it taking the whole derivative; at full membership the derivative passes. The transposes stay the default; the framework's backward is used only with those same local derivatives.
- **Rule 37, with §19.49.** `interpret` takes the most active word concept; among equals the largest (§19.30), then the one found first.
- **Rule 39.** The place row's dimming is read at a token's first place (or applied once to its reading), never at each byte's own place inside the product. The row's magnitude is carried by the Sigma's weight on it.
- **Rule 41.** One where, both rungs, and say the capacity: with the registry's capacity the short rung separates a sentence's words and the long rung removes the short rung's repeats. And the binding by token does not know order, so anagrams and letters contained in a longer word read as the word; either the ordered run that §19.48 answer 4 set aside returns, or a word row takes its letters at their places within the token.
- **Rules 35 and 38.** The trial of §20.8 suggests what `attend` learns first is small: where the next place is, from where the last word ended.

`test/test_item17_looks_prototype.py` (9 passed, 3.9 s). The tables are `test/looks_prototype_report.py`'s output (deterministic; its random activities use a generator of its own). Item 1.8's third default sweep (1.8 §66.15) included `test_item17_looks_prototype.py` and ended with no failure.

## 21. Item 1.7: the rules in one place (Claude, 2026-11-19)

Alec, 2026-11-19: "Write the rules of item 1.7 once, as one clean
statement of the perceptual basis and the looks ... Mark what is mine,
what is yours, and what is open." This section states every rule of
item 1.7 once, as it stands after §19.52 to §19.64. For the build it
replaces §19.21 and §19.51; those sections and the ones around them
are its record, and where they differ this section stands. Nothing
here is new: each rule names where it was decided.

**The marks.**

- *(Alec, §n)* after a rule's name: the rule is his decision, and the
  section holds his words.
- *Mine:* a reading or a default of Claude's. It is built as written
  and is his to change.
- *Open:* not settled. What is built meanwhile is said, and the round
  that builds it reports it.

Rules 1 to 42 keep the numbers they had. Rules 43 to 49 are new
numbers for what §19.53 to §19.65 decided.

**What it builds.** One structure at every order: a Pi, then Not, then
a Sigma. Percepts, and above order zero symbols, are unsigned rows of
a square, sparse Pi, a product of memberships. Concepts are signed and
are a Sigma over them, each entry for or Not. A row exists only when
MTM nominates it. Symbols are split from concepts and have no
dimensions. A form's code is the set of its parts, so that one form is
a part of another exactly when its code lies inside the other's. A
sentence's percepts are read once into one bank, and a look is an
activity over that bank: `attend` asks for concepts, the request is
carried down as a salience map onto what each percept is and onto
where it stands, and what the way up then gives is what `interpret`
chooses from. The old classes are not edited.

**A. The layers and the structure.**

1. *New classes* (Alec, §18.24, rule 32). `PiLayer3` and `SigmaLayer3`
   (*mine:* the names). `SigmaLayer`, `PiLayer`, `PiLayer2` and
   `SigmaLayer2` are not edited, and nothing built with them changes
   value.
2. *The Pi* (Alec, §18.24, rules 21 and 31). Square and sparse, on
   unsigned values: $z = \exp(W \log \mathrm{clamp}(m, \epsilon, 1) + b)$,
   with `PiLayer2`'s constraints (diagonal at one or more, the rest at
   zero or more, bias at zero or less), so a row requires the members
   it has weight on and never exceeds its own reading. Its way back is
   the exact LDU solve. *Mine:* each percept or symbol is two unsigned
   rows, one for each lane (a reading of §18.25); a row has weight
   only on rows of its own lane (a reading of rule 29); and its
   derivative passes wherever a membership lies between the floor and
   one, one included, where `PiLayer2`'s clamp passes none at exactly
   one (§19.64, point 6).
3. *The Sigma* (Alec, §18.24, rule 23; §18.25; rule 29; "Signed sigma;
   good, this is knowing in the signed hyperball"). For each concept
   one signed number, $\tanh(x\,U)$, in $[-1, 1]$. Each input has one
   signed weight. Its positive part is the input's *for entry* and its
   negative part is its *Not entry*, so an entry is never both. A
   weight starts at zero or above (rules 8b and 21), so there is no
   Not entry until teaching makes one. The concept's value is stored
   as two unsigned lanes, its positive part on the for lane and its
   negative part on the against lane; a single reading is never
   "both". *Mine:* it has no bias; where an answer is read from a
   Sigma, the signed number is read. *Since rule 63* (which withdraws
   rule 59): the Sigma is monotone. Each entry has one weight, held
   at zero or above, on the one signed value the Not gives for its
   input. A Not entry is an entry of the Not and not a weight below
   zero of the Sigma: it exchanges that input's pair for that
   concept, and the Sigma's weight on it is again at zero or above.
   The gradient may carry an entry through zero, which makes it a
   Not entry (§19.91); the weight, its size, is never below zero.
4. *The cycle* (Alec, §18.25, as amended by rules 20, 21, 26 and
   63). At an order with $n$ concepts: $n$ signed values, stored as
   $2n$ unsigned lanes; the rows above that MTM has nominated read
   those lanes, each row its own lane; the Not joins each symbol's
   pair into one signed value, for less against, and the next Sigma
   reads those signed values (rule 63).
29. *One structure: Pi, Not, Sigma, at every order* (Alec, §19.20).
    - *At the basic level* the Pi reads perceptual space and makes
      the basic percepts, each row with its two values, for and
      against; the Not joins each row's two values into one signed
      value; the Sigma reads those signed values, sparse, with
      weights at zero or above (rules 62 and 63). A Not entry there
      is from one row to one concept. It records that something
      expected is absent: "animal cognition sees particular events
      not happening, but it does not negate ideas". What teaches it
      is an omission, the concept expected and not come ("Omission
      teaches not: yes, for percepts, the opposite of 1 is 0, not -1,
      as in Boole").
    - *Above it,* for a mind that has symbols, the structure repeats:
      a Pi makes symbols over concepts, a Not entry is from one
      symbol to one concept (the concept reads that symbol's pair
      swapped), and a Sigma makes the concepts. What tells a human
      mind from an animal's is this recursion, which symbols enable,
      and not the Not.
    - The operator `not` of a sentence or a thought swaps the lanes
      of what it is put on (`FieldLogic.reduce`), as now. It can be
      put on any symbol, and no omission need teach it.
    - The Not alone changes a sign (rule 63; Alec, §19.90). With no
      Not entry read, a mind speaks only of what is (§19.15).

**B. The perceptual basis: a form, its code and its way back.**

5. *A percept's code obeys the mereology* (Alec, §18.24, rule 27): at
   or above each part's code and at or below each whole's. For a form
   it is so by construction, since a form's code is the join of its
   parts' codes (rule 43). *Mine:* where a row is not a form coded by
   its parts (a configuration with `identityByParts` off, or the
   fallback by bytes), its code is the greatest over its parts' codes
   and a small draw keyed to the row, in place of the sum of its
   bytes' codes (`BytesFallbackEncoder.encode`), as §19.21 had it.
43. *The part map: a form's code is the set of its parts* (Alec,
    §19.54, §19.56).
    - A part is a run of adjacent characters. The parts of a form are
      its characters and the longer parts that exist and lie inside
      it.
    - *The space is a character,* a part like a letter, "so that the
      saliency map can select against it from within parts". A form
      may hold one (`ice cream`).
    - *No end marks.* A form's code does not mark its first and its
      last character. So a form has one code wherever it stands: `is`
      alone and `is` inside `this`.
    - *A longer part exists only where it is needed* ("we should also
      do pairs only when needed"). The map starts from the
      characters. A part of any length, pairs included, is added only
      where two forms would otherwise have the same parts.
    - *A part once added is carried by every form that holds that
      run,* the forms admitted before it and those admitted after.
      Otherwise a form with the part would stop reading as inside a
      longer form that holds it.
    - *Every percept whole inside a form is a part of it* (Alec,
      §19.119: "reach does not halls all of archers parts, "her" is
      a part. We need a powerset of percept wholes to
      differentiate"). A stored form that lies inside a form as a
      run is one of its parts, with a part of its own in the map;
      so is the run of parts of a row. Two forms of the same
      characters are then told apart by the wholes they hold, and
      the order of a run is kept (§19.119, 6). *Mine:* where one
      form still holds every part of another without holding it as
      a run, each gets a run the other does not hold.
    - So parthood is read from the codes: a form found inside a form
      lies wholly inside its code. What makes something a word is no
      longer in the code; it is the level a request asks for (rule
      35).
    - *Mine:* the part added for two forms is the shortest run that
      one of them holds and the other does not. The exact code is
      the list of the form's parts (`WordIdentity.words`), and the
      row of fixed width is its fold, each part's fixed bits joined
      (`WordIdentity.atom_code`, `form`), in the layout's width as it
      is: no configuration is resized. Where two forms' rows are
      still the same after a part is added, the part's bits are
      raised as `WordIdentity._mint` raises a mint's today.
    - *Mine, and open:* the lengths 1 to n of today's code go. A
      length is not a part, and with the lengths kept `banana` and
      `bananana` would need no part to tell them apart, where his
      example adds one. The 32 coordinates of the length block stay
      in the layout and hold nothing for a form. *Open:* what they
      become (§19.54, point 3).
    - *Open, from round 1 (§23.1.1):* two forms whose parts differ and
      whose rows of fixed width are the same. Built: they share the
      row, and the form admitted first keeps its key (120 of 19,821
      words; none in the lesson). Recommended to Alec: the part block
      takes the 32 empty coordinates.
6. *A basic percept is a row of the Pi* over its parts and wholes
   (Alec, §18.5, rule 8, with rule 31), in place of the least of
   `BasicPercepts.read`. For order zero, `store.conjunctive` and the
   key `conceptualPi` go. It becomes a row when MTM nominates it (rule
   20). *Mine (§23.3.4):* in a basic percept's row the run of parts
   is the percept's presence. It is read as present wherever it lies
   in the extent, and it stands the same on both lanes, since a run
   of parts has no against of its own. The wholes are read on their
   own lanes and must hold over the extent. So a percept whose parts
   are there and whose whole is witnessed not to hold reads against
   (the character `7` under the property "capital": for 0, against
   1). As first built the against lane was the product of the
   members' against lanes, which the run of parts made zero.
   *Amended again (§23.3.5):* a row's value reads its wholes where
   its run lies, not over the whole reading, so a space elsewhere in
   a sentence is not evidence against a word; and its against lane
   is the union of its wholes' against lanes, since one whole
   witnessed not to hold denies the row. A row is then for or
   against, and both stands across the rows of a reading.
44. *The lookup of a sentence's forms, on the device* (Alec, §19.55,
    §19.57; §19.64, point 2). The parts of a sentence are found at
    every place by one product for each character length. The word is
    then found from its parts by its set of parts as an address: one
    probe, and no product against every form (0.76 ms a sentence for
    both stages on Metal, against 6.25 ms). *Mine, on his "Up to you
    when":* this is built in item 1.5, with results equal to this
    item's. In this item the store's lookup stays as it is
    (`RadixLayer.lookup_with_id`: the dictionary, the trie's longest
    match, the fallback by bytes), it is made once for a sentence,
    and the first Pi is read only on the rows it names (rule 33).
45. *The way back of a form starts from the form alone* (Alec,
    §19.58: "we are not always doing reconstruction: sometimes we do
    generation"). No place of a part is taken from a read. "The whole
    stores its parts in order, and longest first"; the read's matrix
    of a form's parts stays binary and has no order. *Mine:* in this
    item the stored order is the table the source keeps, a form's
    characters in order (`RadixLayer.inverse_table`), which is his
    alternative with the letters as the parts. The table of the
    longest parts, half its size and equal in result, is built with
    the device tables of item 1.5. What goes now is the spelling
    rebuilt from the end-marked pairs and the greatest length
    (`WordIdentity.read_parts`, `assemble_pairs`), which cannot stand
    without end marks: its callers read the stored table, and a code
    that is no stored form has no spelling.
46. *A string read as a word it is not is taught when it is observed*
    (Alec, §19.64, point 3). Nothing is added to a form's code or to
    the match for it: no length that has to agree, and no match at
    every place. The teaching is an idempotent round over cases
    gathered from the training harness's logs. What is admitted is
    the part that discriminates the string from the word, and not the
    string (Alec, §19.65: "We don't want to admit Felixx, we want to
    admit the part that discriminates it from Felix: "xx""). *Mine:*
    the part is the shortest run that the string holds and the word
    does not, rule 43's own step; the string gets no row; once the
    part exists, the parts found in the string are no longer exactly
    the word's, so it is not read as the word wherever a word is the
    form whose parts are exactly those found (rule 44). Admitting a
    part that exists changes nothing. The store's side is this item's
    (certificate 28). The harness's log of a word put back as another
    word, and the round that gathers the cases, are item 1.6's.

**C. Order zero.**

7. *Combination within one reading* (Alec, §18.24, rule 22; §19.17;
   ""Pi on the gaps". You mean pi over the individual percept dims
   instead of pooling? Good."). For each lane, the vectors of the
   active percepts are combined into one vector as wide as the
   perceptual space, and the Sigma reads the for vector less the
   against vector. The combination is, for each dimension, a Pi over
   the percepts of the reading, taken on one less each value:
   $x_i = 1 - \prod_p (1 - v_{p,i})^{b_p}$, with $b_p$ the Pi's value
   for percept $p$ on that lane and $v_p$ its full vector. `.where`
   and `.when` are read unsigned; since item 1.8 they are stored so
   (1.8 §59.62), and a reader of an angle takes $2x - 1$. The `.where`
   of a reading is not combined over its percepts (Alec, §19.67:
   "It's own, flowing from the fixed .where parameter we mentioned").
   A reading has one place, its own, and its where wires come from
   the where parameter of rule 47. Combined over the percepts they
   say how many percepts there are and no longer where (round 2,
   §23.2.1: 0 of 48 places read). It is read at the degree that the
   reading is present. *Mine (§23.S.1):* the Sigma of order zero does
   not read the `.when`. Claude first had it read like the `.where`;
   a concept then learned a weight on the clock, and a trained
   answer changed with the tick.
8. *The concepts of order zero* (Alec, §18.24, rule 23): the Sigma of
   rule 3 on $x$, with $U$ dense, of the perceptual width by the
   concepts. It replaces the fold of `ConceptualSpace._compose_order0`,
   the readout `IndexedSigmaConceptsFromPercepts`, and item 1.8's
   stand-in for one signed weight (`SparseLayer._fold_weights`) at
   order zero.

8b. *A concept made at order zero starts from its members* (*mine*):
   a new column of $U$, the sum over its members of each member's
   vector divided by that vector's squared length,
   $u = \sum_k v_k / |v_k|^2$ (a Not member subtracted), which the
   network then learns; under rule 21 a new concept has one member,
   its own row. So a concept reads each of its members at one or
   more before the squash, and another reading by the share of a
   member's vector that the reading holds. A member that joins later
   is added to the column in the same way, and nothing is normalized
   afterwards. (Until §23.3.1 this
   said "normalized". At unit length a row of 60 ones reads 7.7
   before the squash, and the eight word concepts of the lesson each
   read every word at .9999986 and more.) What promotion, `PerceptCollections.collect`
   and the lessons write today (an edge in the feature matrix,
   `add_concept_feature`) becomes such a column. The Pi of order zero
   holds only the mereology's entries, a percept over its parts and
   wholes; no concept writes into it, and it stays full rank.

**D. Above order zero.**

9. *Symbols are split from concepts and have no dimensions* (Alec,
   §18.22, rules 14, 15 and 20). Separate tensors; a symbol has no
   vector, place, form or trust content read as a direction; the
   shared row of a concept and its symbol is given up. It has no
   address in the where registry either (Alec, §19.88: "A symbol
   does not live in any space, which is what makes its collection by
   sigma so set-like").
10. *A symbol is two unsigned rows, one for each lane, and brings one
    concept* (Alec, §18.25; rules 2 and 21), which is how it starts
    and not a limit (rule 21, §19.94). The symbols have a table of
    their own, with their own index and the record of the concept
    each brought (`SymbolTable`, §23.4.4). *Withdrawn (§19.101):*
    Claude's sentence that a declared concept has its symbol made at
    its declaration; no symbol is made for a concept (rule 71). It
    is made when MTM
    nominates it (rule 20), or by `interpret` for a meta concept, and
    not at a concept's allocation. A conjunction is promoted as a new
    symbol, a Pi row over its members, under a new concept, a Sigma
    over that symbol. *How each is made* (Alec, §19.88: "Symbols are
    implicitly created by PI, concepts are implicitly created by
    sigma. Symbols and concepts are explicitly created by MTM"):
    from a statement that two are the same ("Felix is my cat") MTM
    makes or finds one symbol for both; from a statement of kind or
    of part ("Felix is a cat") it makes a link of member to kind or
    of part to whole, by the orders of the two (rule 21, and
    `doc/Orders.md` on what raises an order). "Since implicit
    generally preceeds explicit, MTM should check for an existing
    fit first": before it makes a symbol or a concept, MTM looks for
    one that the Pi or the Sigma has already made and that fits.
11. *The Sigma above order zero* (Alec, §18.24, rule 24, with
    §18.25): it reads each symbol's pair combined into one signed
    input. No vector and no pooling. *Mine:* stored sparse.
12. *Sigma and Pi at every order* (Alec, §18.24, rule 25). The least
    and the greatest of `SparseLayer.fold_presence` go above order
    zero too, and item 1.8's `SparseLayer._fold_weights` with them.
13. *Place and time* (Alec, §18.24, rule 26). A percept's vector
    carries `.where` and `.when`; a symbol stores neither; its
    `.where` is written when STM reads it. Where a product reads them
    they are taken unsigned (rule 7).
14. *Between conceptual orders, only activation* (Alec, §18.22, rule
    16): a pull within one order does not pass through a symbol.

**E. Learning and the way back.**

15. *Membership is learned under a penalty* (Alec, §18.24, rule 29;
    rule 22). *Mine:* §18.3's penalty, measured first, on the Pi's
    entries and on the Sigma's entries above order zero. A
    promotion writes an entry at one into capacity allocated
    beforehand, at order zero as above it (rule 62). The penalty
    thins the values of entries that exist; with rule 67, if its
    trial holds, the same penalty says when an entry is written and
    when one is removed, at order zero too.
16. *Likeness of codes pairs nothing* (*mine*, from §18.24, rule 28).
    A row enters a set, or two rows are taken as neighbours, by the
    mereology or by a promotion, never by the likeness of their
    codes. The readers that decide by likeness today are §19.4, list
    1, and the table of §19.21.
17. *The way back* (Alec, §18.24, rule 30; §19.24). The Pi inverts
    exactly; the Sigma returns the combined vector by least squares
    where there are enough concepts, and not otherwise. A signed
    value on the way back is replaced by its two unsigned parts
    before a percept or a symbol holds it, as on the way up: -.5 is
    .5 on the against lane and nothing on the for lane. Teaching does
    not assume an exact inverse; where it does today is §19.4, list
    2.

**F. The learned maps of System 1, and storage.**

18. *The stacks are the same structure* (Alec, §19.10; rule 29). A
    fused pair, `SigmaPiLayer` (new: no class of that name is in the
    source), and `SigmaPiStack` (`expect`, the read from a field to a
    point, and the marker of `bin/Language.py`) are pairs of rules 2
    and 3, a Pi and then a Sigma whose entries are for or Not, with
    no way back, fused so that a stack is captured as one graph.
    Today `bin/SigmaPiStack.py` uses `PiLayer`'s chart of odds and a
    linear `SigmaLayer` clipped to 0 to 1. Rules 6 and 7 of §18.5
    stand for the rest (the keys, the pair count, the seed, the last
    Sigma starting at zero, the cost of an MLP layer). `expectLayers`
    and `ideaLayers` stay at 1, and `markerLayers` at 2. *Mine:* the
    stacks read concepts, which are scalars (§19.19); and the clip to
    0 to 1 goes with the old arithmetic, since rule 3's Sigma gives
    one signed number in -1 to 1 (§19.64, point 6).
19. *The matrices are tensors on the device* (*mine*): the Pi and the
    Sigma above order zero are stored as compressed rows, not as
    dictionaries of edges (`SparseLayer._index`), and grow into
    capacity allocated beforehand. They can be read by row and by
    column (rule 28), with an index of columns kept beside the rows.

**G. Rows and concepts** (§19.10).

20. *MTM nominates every row of the Pi* (Alec). A basic percept at
    order zero, and a symbol at every order above it, becomes a row
    only when MTM nominates it on recurrence (`concept_mint_count`);
    nothing becomes a row on its first reading. *Mine:* the tower of
    parts and wholes below the basic percepts is perception and is
    made on first sight, as now. *Mine (§23.3.1):* for the count, a
    reading is one sentence of one stream, so a form that stands
    twice in a sentence is read once; and there is one count, kept by
    MTM under the form, that every reader of the form adds to. A
    reading is one forward of the model for one stream, named by a
    serial that `begin_reading` advances (`ConceptualSpace.reading`),
    so that every reader of a form in that forward counts once
    (§23.3.5). This
    replaces the basic percept
    reserved at a word's first reading (`BasicPercepts.reserve` in
    the word loop of `bin/Models.py`), the lessons' declared
    admission (`Corpus.admit_training_forms`,
    `ConceptLessons.admit_native_forms`), and symbols made at a
    concept's allocation.
    - *A new word* is perceived at once, but `interpret` cannot find
      it until its basic percept is nominated; its concept comes with
      that row (Alec, "A,b,c,d, yes").
    - *Not nominated* (Alec): the meta concept of a word and its
      object, which `interpret` makes, with its structure, when it
      interprets the word and the meta concept does not yet exist;
      the blank object, below; and the grammar's declared concepts,
      the 72 arguments and 27 operator classes of §19.9, each
      declared with its row at construction.
    - *The 12 frozen thought predicates* of §19.9 stay columns of $U$
      at zero, frozen, read by thought as references and never by
      perception (Alec, "E nice!").
    - *The blank object* (Alec). For a word with no object,
      `interpret` makes a new concept with no members, together with
      the meta concept; today MTM holds such a word as a pending name
      (`InterpretLayer.reading`, `pool.named`). Its vector starts at
      zero ("Pure zero is even better, since magnitude is certainty
      in that space"); a read that normalizes a concept vector must
      not divide by its zero length. *Mine:* it is one order above
      its word.
21. *One concept for each row, to start with* (Alec). Each nominated
    row brings one concept, which starts reading only its own row,
    at one: at order zero, its entry on that row (rule 62). The room
    is §19.83's: order zero has as many concepts as basic percepts,
    and each order above half the one below. *A start and not a
    limit* (Alec, §19.94: "please do not enforce that one percept or
    symbol goes to one concept, or that the subsequent PI must
    collect one sigma (as before)"): a row or a symbol may be read by
    any number of concepts, by its value or its not-value (rule 63);
    a concept may read any number of rows or symbols; a row of the
    Pi above may read any number of concepts. Nothing in the source
    shares an index between a symbol and a concept or takes "the"
    concept of a row where there may be several. Which concept a
    row brought is a record made at its nomination
    (`ConceptAllocator.brought`), and nothing infers it. Concepts have no
    nomination or promotion of their own: MTM's promotions of
    classes, identities and percept collections become nominations of
    rows. The one writer of a concept's further inputs stays: a kept
    reading adds the word that filled an argument to that argument
    (`ConceptHierarchy.observe_member`), as an entry on the word's
    symbol once MTM has nominated it.
22. *Both thinned* (Alec). Rule 15's penalty is on the Sigma's
    entries above order zero as well as on the Pi's; §19.13 shows
    that with the Pi alone penalized what is learned cannot be read
    from the rows. The structure of a meta concept is never thinned.
    *Mine:* a definition between concepts ("balloons are rubber", an
    edge taught from its `LTM1` part row by `DefinitionFold`) stays
    under the penalty, held by its witness's cost.

**H. The vertical spread** (§19.11).

23. *A fan up and a share down* (Alec), on the structure's own
    matrices, Pi and Sigma alike, by the size of their weights. Up: a
    concept's or a symbol's value is split among the rows that read
    it, each by its weight's share of all the weights it is read with
    (its fan). Down: a row's value is split among its inputs, each by
    its weight's share of the row. What a row receives is summed over
    all its parents and children, at most one; a Not entry passes to
    the other lane. At order zero the way down goes on into the first
    layer (rule 30); the combined vector of order zero's Sigma is not
    passed (rule 17).
24. *Siblings get less than the concept that caused them* (Alec). A
    concept present at one gives every other concept the spread
    reaches less than one.
25. *One pass, written to the expected field at every order, where
    the grammar calls for it* (Alec, §19.22). Up once, then down
    once, from order zero's expectation (`expect`) and the observed
    field. It writes `_expected_knowing` at every order, where
    `ConceptSpread.open_prediction` writes order zero alone today. It
    is what `intuit` runs after it deposits expect's field; expect
    itself is the map at order zero alone, and a model with no
    symbols never runs the spread over the orders. *Mine:* it also
    runs at the end of the read, before comprehension takes its
